verdict_reason: The conception is the best thing I have reviewed in this pack — a genuine free body where the car is the prime mover and the runtime only watches is exactly right, and the reasoning chain that lands the port in the sidewall with its outer edge on CAVITY_RADIUS (so the sill IS the floor) is airtight and verified in the node data. But I walked the loop against the collision mesh instead of the prose, and it does not open. The boarding gangway — the object the entire entry sequence depends on — is a pure Blender Mesh with no nodes and no triangles, so the drivable surface stops dead at the dock edge (|x|=4.45, z=0.78) with a void before the sill. Behind that void, one collision band (upp_r↔shl_r) was never cut by the port, leaving an invisible 1.14 m barricade standing across the doorway. You cannot get in. And if you could, the cage is ~60x too stiff for its deliberately-reduced mass, so the crown deflects 3 mm where it needs 235 mm to make a contact patch: the Colossus stands on a ~0.8 m strip with a 1.6-degree tip angle, well under the gyroscopic stability speed for a 14 m radius hoop. It lies down. Then there is a whole tier of designed-but-unwired feel: insideTire is dead, so "get out again" has no beat at all; exit_warn_deg=52 is dead, so the only exit callout fires when the 1.2-second window is already open; b.best is written and never shown. This is a magnificent object with a loop that has never been driven. Fix the two entry defects, the stiffness, and the torque double-count and I think it becomes extraordinary — the bones are all there.
excellent: The physics honesty, and fitAxle in spec.LUA_BEHAVIOR. A three-point circle fit gives centre, plane and rotation with zero assumption about how far the tire has rolled or which way it faces, and it keeps working 300 m from the dock. Nothing applies force or pose. Do not touch this — it is the reason the whole idea is worth building.

The port siting argument in spec.py. Ruling out the bead holes (6.72 m off the ground plus a 5.8 m interior drop) and the tread (pinched shut exactly when it is at ground level) and landing on the sidewall with PORT_OUTER_RADIUS = CAVITY_RADIUS so the sill is dead flush with the floor. I verified it: lin_r_j00 sits at z=0.934, exactly CAVITY_FLOOR_Z. No lip, by construction.

The straps. Two real beams carrying extra.breakGroup='colossus_tiedown', wired to beamstate.breakBreakGroup, load-bearing at spawn and visibly modelled. This is a real tie-down, not a fabricated connector to satisfy a graph check.

DOCK_CLEAR_X = 4.450 against SECTION_HALF = 4.200 as a hard keep-out, with the gangway hanging off the TIRE so nothing fixed is inside the sweep volume. That is a real level-design insight and it is the right answer.

PORT_STATIONS = 4 landing the port centred exactly on station 0, which is exactly the bottom (bead_r_j00 at y=0, z=6.72 = 14.086-7.366). It makes markerAngle's angleZero genuinely mean 'port at bottom', so portClock is correct by construction rather than by tuning.

The cavity floor curvature is well sized and nobody should touch CAVITY_RADIUS for feel reasons. Sagitta on 13.153 m radius is 75 mm across a 2.7 m wheelbase and 194 mm out to the nose at 2.25 m — a gentle dish the car rides, not a bowl it beaches in. Dock grade 7.1% over 8.4 m width is likewise correct and unfussy.

findings.title: The boarding gangway has no collision — the drive surface ends in a void
findings.problem: build_tongue() creates only Mesh objects (tongue, tongue_kerb, tongue_ribs). The handoff has zero nodes with a 'tongue' prefix and zero triangles referencing one — I enumerated all 976 nodes and all 2838 triangles. BeamNG flexbodies are visual only; collision comes from `triangles`. So the drivable surface is: dock deck fixed nodes out to |x|=4.450 at z=0.780, then NOTHING, then the liner at |x|<=3.600, z=0.934. The car drives off a 0.78 m cliff into a 0.81 m trench with the far side 0.153 m higher, and wedges between the dock face and the tire's shoulder. The premise sentence in spec.py — 'a steel boarding tongue bolted to the port sill... Parked, it bridges continuously' — is true of the render and false of the physics.
findings.fix: Give the tongue real free nodes on the tire cage. Add a 3 x 5 node grid (15 nodes on a 960-node cage, nothing) spanning from the port sill ring out to TONGUE_REACH_X=4.760, beamed into lin_r/upp_r/shl_r at the port stations with the port_frame spec, and emit its triangles with ground_model 'metal'. Bevel the tip so the 50 mm TONGUE_TIP_THICK lip ramps to zero over the last 0.30 m instead of presenting a square edge at x=4.760. Then add a generator assertion that the collision surface is continuous in z from DOCK_LANDING_Z to CAVITY_FLOOR_Z along y=0 — this class of defect must not be able to ship again.

findings.title: Port cut missed a collision band: invisible 1.14 m barricade in the doorway
findings.where: examples/giant_props/colossus_tire/blender/create_colossus_tire.py — port cut in the cage builder; spec.PORT_OUTER_RADIUS
findings.problem: Three sidewall bands are cut over the port stations (46,47,00,01): low_r-max_r, max_r-upp_r and lin_r-shl_r all carry 176 triangles instead of 192. The upp_r-shl_r band carries the full 192 — it is uncut. At the bottom that band runs from (|x|=3.637, z=0.470) to (|x|=4.019, z=1.142), a 60-degree panel standing across the full 30 degrees of the doorway, its top edge 0.208 m ABOVE the sill and 0.42 m outboard of it. Root cause: PORT_OUTER_RADIUS = CAVITY_RADIUS = 13.153 falls BETWEEN two meridian rings (upp_r at 12.944, shl_r at 13.616), so the cut has no node ring to land on radially. spec.py is proud that PORT_SPAN_DEG is a whole number of stations so the opening lands on node columns — that solved the angular alignment only. PORT_INNER_RADIUS was deliberately snapped to MERIDIAN[1]; the outer edge never was.
findings.fix: Insert a meridian station at the port's outer radius so the cut lands on a ring. Fraction = (13.153-7.366)/6.720 = 0.861, so add (0.861, ~0.929) to spec.MERIDIAN between (0.830,0.957) and (0.930,0.866), with a matching SIDEWALL_THICKNESS entry (~0.40), then cut every band between the new sill ring and low_r. Add a generator assertion that PORT_INNER_RADIUS and PORT_OUTER_RADIUS each coincide with a MERIDIAN station radius to within 1 mm.

findings.title: Cage ~60x too stiff for its mass: 1.6 deg tip angle, the tire falls over
findings.problem: TIRE_MASS was cut 61x from an honest 1.91e6 kg to 31,000 kg, but BEAM_SPECS were derived from real material properties at full scale and never rescaled — so the cage is ~60x stiffer relative to its own load than a real tire. Check it: 304 kN of weight over roughly 25 crown nodes in contact against tread beamSpring 3.0e6 gives ~3 mm of radial deflection. CROWN_DROP is 0.235 m, so the crown needs 235 mm of deflection to put the 6.72 m tread on the ground and gets 3. Contact half-width = sqrt(2 * 24 * 0.0033) = 0.40 m. Static tip angle = atan(0.40/14.086) = 1.63 degrees. Gyroscopic stabilisation does not rescue it either — v_crit is O(sqrt(gR)) = ~12 m/s minimum for a 14.086 m radius hoop, and the design target is 8.33 m/s. This is not a tire, it is a 28 m steel hoop balancing on a knife edge, and updateTipped's 'reset the prop to stand it back up' message tells me the design already suspected it.
findings.fix: Rescale the whole cage by the same factor the mass was: divide every beamSpring and beamDamp in BEAM_SPECS (bead, belt, casing, sidewall, tread, inflation) by ~60, which preserves every damping ratio the docstring argues for. Concretely tread goes 3.0e6 -> 5.0e4, sized so the contact deflects ~0.25 m under the tire's own 304 kN — that gives contact half-width sqrt(2*24*0.25) = 3.46 m, i.e. the full TREAD_HALF=3.36 in contact and a 13.4-degree tip angle. Also drop CROWN_DROP by raising TREAD_ARC_RADIUS from 24.0 to ~56 (drop 0.10 m) so the crown is still realistically arced but reachable. Then assert the achieved static contact half-width in the generator, the way MASS_TOTAL_TOLERANCE is asserted.

findings.title: The mass derivation double-counts torque — 31 t should be ~15.5 t
findings.problem: The solve adds 'torque from the occupant's weight moment' (87.2 kNm) to 'torque from its driven-axle traction' (92.9 kNm) for 180.1 kNm. These are the same torque counted twice. The only forces the car applies to the tire are a normal force (radial — zero moment arm about the axle, contributes nothing) and a friction force f (tangential, torque f*R_cavity). The weight moment is not a second torque; it is what determines f in equilibrium: holding station at climb angle phi requires f = m*g*sin(phi), and the traction ceiling is f <= 0.45*m*g*cos(phi) for a 50/50 2WD car at mu 0.9. Those two are equal at tan(phi)=0.45, phi=24.2 deg — which is exactly why the spec's two numbers came out at 87 and 93. Real available torque is ~90 kNm, not 180.
findings.fix: Redo the solve with T = 90 kNm: I_admissible = 90e3/0.0394 = 2.28e6 kg m^2, and at the stated radius of gyration 12.15 m that is TIRE_MASS = 15,500 kg. Keep the 30 km/h in 15 s target and change the number, or keep 31,000 kg and restate the target honestly as ~30 s. Do not ship 31 t against a 15 s claim — at 31 t the player pumps a perfect 24-degree climb for half a minute in the dark before anything happens, and that is where they quit.

findings.title: The cavity is unlit and unmarked — the whole second half of the loop happens blind
findings.where: examples/giant_props/colossus_tire/spec.py PALETTE (liner entry) and blender/create_colossus_tire.py:385 build of liner_crown/liner_fillet
findings.problem: The liner is albedo [0.088,0.092,0.086] — near black — inside a closed torus whose only aperture is the port, and the port is the thing that rotates away. grep finds zero 'emissive' and zero JBEAM_PROPS in the entire mod. The cabin.jpg render is honest that it is 'lit by a render-only work lamp'; in game there is no light at all. The liner is also completely featureless: build_liner uses liner_mat everywhere, no markings, and the hazard_chevron material is used only on the tongue and dock kerbs. So once the port passes ~40 degrees the player is driving a black drum with no light, no landmark, no directional cue, no way to judge speed, and no way to find the port again. This is the single change that most improves the mod: everything after 'STRAPS CUT' currently happens where the player cannot see.
findings.fix: The pack already has both mechanisms proven. (1) Add worklights: spec.JBEAM_PROPS with SPOTLIGHT entries on the port bezel firing inward, the same mechanism gforce_centrifuge uses (prop_builder.py:815). Four around the bezel ring. (2) Add an emissive liner marking material to PALETTE — a THREE-component emissiveFactor plus emissiveIntensityNits, per the Round-16/17 photometric law in prop_builder.py:485 — and paint on the liner in the generator: a circumferential lane pair at |x| = +/-2.4, a numbered pitch ladder so speed and distance read at a glance, and a lit chevron ring around the port's inner mouth so the exit is findable from anywhere in the barrel. Mine tyres genuinely are marked and internally lamped for inspection, so none of this costs realism.

findings.title: insideTire() is dead code — 'get out again' has no beat at all
findings.problem: insideTire(tire, vehicle) is defined and never called anywhere — I grepped both the spec and the generated runtime, it has exactly one occurrence in each, its own definition. It is the only mechanism that could detect the player after the tire leaves the dock (the cabin trigger is world-anchored and gated on `not b.released`). Consequence: the climax of the loop — threading the moving port and getting out — produces zero feedback. No 'CLEAR', no final distance, no revolution count, nothing. b.best is likewise written at line 936 and never displayed, and behavior.reset carefully preserves it across resets for no reader. The brief asks specifically about getting out again; right now the game does not know you did.
findings.fix: Call insideTire once per update for the player vehicle after release and track the transition. On inside->outside fire the payoff: showMessage(string.format('CLEAR. %d revolutions, %.0f m.', b.revolutions, b.distance)) plus emitEvent 'colossus_dismounted', and if b.distance > b.best show 'NEW BEST' before overwriting it. On outside->inside allow re-boarding so a player can jump back in for another run without a reset. Show b.best in behavior.reset's message too.

findings.title: Exit warning never wired: the callout fires when the window is already open
findings.problem: The `elseif not open and degrees < B.exit_warn_deg and not b.exitWarned` branch sets b.exitWarned and does nothing else; b.exitWarned is never read and never reset, so exit_warn_deg = 52.0 is a dead constant. The only message the player gets is 'PORT IS DOWN - go now if you want out' at |clock| < 20 degrees. At 8.33 m/s the tire turns 40 degrees in 1.18 s, and the manoeuvre it is asking for is a 90-degree turn in a 7.2 m lane. There is no lead time whatsoever, so the exit is not a skill test, it is a coin flip you are told about too late.
findings.fix: Wire the anticipation. Compute the angular rate from the unwrapped angle (you already have `delta` and dtSim in behavior.update) and call the window by TIME to bottom, not by angle: at ~4 s out show 'PORT COMES ROUND IN 4 - line up now', then tick 3/2/1 as it approaches, then the existing 'PORT IS DOWN'. Reset b.exitWarned each time the window closes so it re-arms every revolution instead of firing once ever. Pair this with the lit chevron ring from the lighting finding so the callout and the visual agree.

findings.title: The 90-degree turn clears the far wall by 60 mm, against 0.46 m vertical curbs
findings.problem: The lane is 7.2 m of flat liner bounded by the lin_r->shl_r fillet, which in the collision mesh rises 0.463 m over 0.037 m of x — a vertical 0.46 m curb, well above a car's 0.3 m wheel radius, so it catches rather than lets the car ride up. Turn geometry for the reference 2.0 x 4.5 m car (wheelbase 2.7, front overhang 0.85, min turn radius ~5.2): the outer front corner sweeps sqrt((5.2+1.0)^2 + 3.55^2) = 7.14 m inboard of the rear-axle position at turn start. Starting with the rear axle exactly on the sill and the whole rear overhang hanging out of the doorway over a void, the corner reaches |x| = -3.54 against a wall at -3.60. Sixty millimetres, at full lock, first try, in the dark. Everything else in this spec is solved from a requirement — TIRE_MASS from an acceleration target, TONGUE_TIP_RADIUS from the landing height — but LINER_HALF is authored and it is the number that decides whether the loop's central manoeuvre works.
findings.fix: Do not widen the lane (the meridian will not give it to you). Instead make the boundary rideable: rebuild the shoulder fillet as a ~1.2 m radius quarter-round from the liner edge up to shl_r instead of a 0.46 m step in 0.037 m, which is what a real tyre shoulder looks like anyway and converts 60 mm of margin into roughly 0.8 m by letting the outer front wheel climb 0.3-0.5 m during the turn. Then add a derivation comment beside LINER_HALF stating the swept-corner requirement (7.14 m for the reference car) and assert the achieved usable width against it.

findings.title: Distance and speed are unsigned path length — rocking in place inflates the score
findings.problem: `travelled = (tire.centre - b.lastCentre):length()` is a 3D magnitude, so it accumulates the axle's vertical bob and any lateral drift, and it is unsigned — rolling the tire BACK toward the dock adds to b.distance exactly like rolling forward. The 0.0005 m/frame gate is only 0.03 m/s at 60 Hz, which a 976-node soft body's cage noise will exceed at rest, so b.speed sits on a nonzero jitter floor and the speed-band callouts can latch off noise. '312 m of ground' can be 312 m of rocking.
findings.fix: Flatten and sign it. Take `local d = tire.centre - b.lastCentre; d.z = 0` for the speed magnitude, and accumulate b.distance as the signed projection onto the rolling direction (axis cross world-up). Better still for the brag number, report the horizontal distance from b.startCentre — 'how far from the dock' is what a player actually wants. Raise the gate to ~0.005 m/frame so cage noise cannot band-trigger.

findings.title: Release fires while the car still straddles the doorway on the gangway
findings.problem: dimensions are full size (blender_kit.py:253 halves them for the object scale), so the cabin box is x in [-3.3, 3.3]. It fires the moment the car's nose crosses |x|=3.3, when the rear 4.5 m of the car is still in the doorway and on the tongue. Three seconds later the straps cut. Because the tongue rides with the TIRE by design, the first inch of tire motion lifts the gangway out from under the car's rear wheels while the car is still on it. Once the tongue has collision (blocker 1) this becomes a guaranteed wreck rather than the dramatic beat it wants to be.
findings.fix: Shrink the cabin trigger's x dimension to ~2.0 (x in [-1.0, 1.0]) so release requires the car fully inboard of the doorway with its tail clear of the sill, or gate cutStraps on the subject's rearmost point being at |x| < 3.0. Keep release_countdown at 3.0 — the anticipation length is right, it is the arming condition that is wrong.

findings.title: The countdown never says 3
findings.problem: b.countdown starts at exactly 3.0 and the message only fires on a change in math.ceil. The first frame takes it to 2.983, whose ceil is still 3, so '3...' is never shown. The player hears 'SUBJECT ABOARD' then '2...' then '1...'. The release beat is the emotional centre of the boarding sequence and it reads as starting mid-count.
findings.fix: Set B.release_countdown to 3.001, or emit the opening tick explicitly in behavior.onEnter alongside the 'SUBJECT ABOARD' message. Given how good this beat is otherwise, it is worth the one line.

findings.title: Dock guardrails and kerbs have no collision — you drive through them
findings.where: examples/giant_props/colossus_tire/authoring handoff: only 6 dock triangles exist (dock_l_0..3 / dock_r_0..3)
findings.problem: The dock's entire collision is 3 quads forming the flat deck. The handrails, posts, kerbs and hazard chevrons that make dock.jpg read as a real quay are visual only, so the player drives straight through the guardrail and off the 0.78 m edge. On the approach that is a mild immersion break; at the port mouth it removes the only thing steering the player into the doorway.
findings.fix: Add fixed nodes for the two kerb lines (DOCK_KERB_H = 0.30) down both deck edges and triangulate them — six or eight more fixed nodes, and fixed nodes cost nothing. Leave the handrails visual. A 0.30 m kerb is enough to keep a car on the deck and to funnel it at the port without feeling like a wall.

verdict_reason: The build's engineering *reasoning* is genuinely at professional level — the pitch sequence is designed the way a real one is, the rim-width/section-width ratio is lifted straight off a 44.00/59 rim, the meridian gauge distribution is right, and the "no sipes" call is exactly the call a tire person would make. But the two things that decide whether a shape reads as an earthmover at 200 m are wrong, and they are wrong in the same direction: the silhouette and the tread. 8400/80R580 has OD/section-width = 3.354 and rim/section-width = 1.754; a 59/80R63 is 2.67 and 1.067, and a 315/80R22.5 highway drive tire is 3.41 and 1.81. The size code the file trusts as its single source of truth is arithmetically a heavy-truck drive tire scaled up, which is why profile.jpg and hero.jpg read exactly that way. On top of that the tread's net-to-gross at the crown face is 35% (53% if you count the chamfer flanks as land) — a mud-terrain LT number, where E-4 rock haulage is 70-85% net — and the shoulder row is the *narrowest* row on the tire when it should be the widest block on it. Then the lug root flare (0.225 m per side) closes a 0.460 m groove to a 10 mm slot at the floor, which no mould could release and where the 0.33 m stone ejector physically cannot exist. Fixing the size code is close to a two-constant change that also *widens* the driving lane, and the tread table is one rewrite. Do those and this becomes something I would stop and stare at; as it stands I look at it and see a truck tire.
excellent: spec.py PITCH_SEQUENCE is a real pitch sequence, not a shuffle: 36 pitches, 3 ratios, arranged in runs of varying length (2,2,1,2,3,1 zeros) that never step 0->2 directly, giving six aperiodic modulation cycles. Adjacent pitches differing by one step is correct mould-flow and stiffness-continuity practice, and order-6 modulation sits above the ride-relevant orders. Better than most shipped game tires. Do not touch.
spec.py MERIDIAN[0] half-width fraction 0.746 is the 44.00/59 rim-to-section-width relationship of a real 59/80R63, carried through exactly. Whoever wrote that looked it up.

spec.py SIDEWALL_THICKNESS: 0.62 m at the bead and 0.30 m at max section width divide back to 88 mm and 43 mm at reference scale - both dead right for an OTR radial, and thinnest at max width where it has to flex is the correct distribution.

spec.py BUTTRESS_DROP=1.55 puts the bottom of the shoulder-lug wrap at r=12.30 m, above max section width at r=11.398 m. That is exactly where a real earthmover buttress wrap stops, and getting it wrong (wrapping past max width) is the usual mistake.

texture_kit.py tire_laminate: different cord pitch AND diameter per band, with the outer belt pair drawn at a different bias so their sections come out elongated. That is a tire person's texture, not a laminated-worktop stripe. The construction logic is right even though it is applied in the wrong place (see findings).

spec.py: no sipes, with the reasoning stated. An E-4/L-5 lug is a solid block and siping it would be the single loudest tell. The chamfer / tie bar / stone ejector / TWI feature set is the correct replacement vocabulary.

findings.title: Size code produces heavy-truck proportions, not earthmover proportions
findings.problem: 8400/80R580 gives OD/section-width = 28.172/8.400 = 3.354 and rim/section-width = 14.732/8.400 = 1.754. Real 80-series earthmover radials: 59/80R63 is 2.668 and 1.067; 53/80R63 is 2.789 and 1.189. A 315/80R22.5 highway drive tire is 3.41 and 1.81. The Colossus is arithmetically the truck tire. The file also claims to be a scale of a 59/80R63, but the three scale ratios disagree wildly - OD ratio 7.046, section-width ratio 5.605, rim-diameter ratio 9.207 - so it is not a scale of anything; it is an 80-series carcass stretched over a rim 1.6x too big for it. This is the whole reason profile.jpg and hero.jpg read as a truck drive tire before you look at any detail, and it is why the bead hole dominates the front elevation instead of the rubber donut.
findings.fix: SECTION_WIDTH_MM = 10350 and RIM_DIAMETER_IN = 457. That gives SECTION_HEIGHT 8.280, BEAD_RADIUS 5.804, OUTER_RADIUS 14.084, OD 28.168 m (4 mm off the current OD, so nothing downstream of OUTER_RADIUS moves), OD/SW 2.721, rim/SW 1.122 - both inside the 59/80R63 to 53/80R63 band. It also collapses the three scale ratios onto each other: OD 7.045, section width 6.906, rim 7.254, i.e. the tire genuinely becomes a uniform 7x 59/80R63 and the laminate gauges stop being 26% over-thick for the section. Knock-ons are all derived: SECTION_HALF 5.175, TREAD_HALF 4.140, LINER_HALF ~4.44, PORT_INNER_RADIUS 8.288 (a taller port), and DOCK_CLEAR_X must stop being the literal 4.450 and become SECTION_HALF + 0.25. CAVITY_RADIUS, CAVITY_FLOOR_Z and the port sill are unchanged. Gameplay improves too: the cavity lane goes from 7.2 m to 8.9 m.

findings.title: Tread is a traction pattern: 35% net-to-gross at the crown, shoulder row smallest
findings.problem: Measured off the actual generator geometry, not the comment. Across the width the crown faces are 1.090 + 2x0.810 + 2x0.470 = 3.650 m of 6.72 m = 54.3% land (add_lug shrinks every block by LUG_CHAMFER=0.115 per side). Circumferentially (2.431 - 0.620 - 0.230)/2.431 = 65.0%. Net-to-gross at the contact face is 0.543 x 0.650 = 35.3%. Even counting the chamfer flanks as land it is 53%. E-4/L-5 rock haulage runs 70-85% net; a mud-terrain light-truck tire is ~60%. Nothing in E- or L-class is under 60%. The header comment claims '45% void - the deep-lug band', which is both optimistic about the geometry and wrong about the class. Compounding it, the shoulder row is the NARROWEST row on the tire (0.700 m half-span against 1.040 intermediate and 1.320 centre). On every rock-service earthmover the shoulder lug is the largest block on the tread - it takes the impact and cut load and anchors the buttress wrap - so the hierarchy is inverted.
findings.fix: Rewrite the row table in fractions of TREAD_HALF so it survives the size-code fix: TREAD_ROWS = ((0.000, 0.160), (0.246, 0.556), (0.642, 1.000)) and TREAD_GROOVES = ((0.160, 0.246), (0.556, 0.642)), i.e. centre rib 0.320, intermediate 0.310, shoulder 0.358 - shoulder now the widest block. Circumferential void drops 28.6% -> 17.2%. Set LATERAL_GROOVE = 0.360 (lateral void 25.5% -> 14.8%). Net-to-gross becomes 0.828 x 0.852 = 70.5%, dead in the E-4 band. At the current TREAD_HALF=3.360 the grooves come out 0.289 m wide; at the fixed TREAD_HALF=4.140 they are 0.356 m, which is 0.050 m at reference scale against a 0.090 m non-skid - the same groove aspect a real 59/80R63 has.

findings.title: Lug root flare closes the circumferential groove floors to 10-50 mm
findings.problem: levels[0] grows the block by LUG_ROOT_FILLET + LUG_DRAFT = 0.150 + 0.075 = 0.225 m per side at the groove floor. The 0.500 m inner circumferential groove therefore has a 0.050 m floor and the 0.460 m outer groove has a 0.010 m floor, under 0.634 m of depth. Three things break at once: no mould releases a 634 mm deep slot that necks to 10 mm; a groove that shape packs solid with fines on the first pass and never clears; and STONE_EJECTOR_R = 0.165 (a 0.33 m dome) cannot physically exist in a 0.01-0.05 m gap - add_ejector is currently building geometry entirely buried inside the lug roots. Separately, the 'fillet' is not a fillet: levels[0]->levels[1] is a straight 0.150 m run over a 0.150 m rise, a 45-degree chamfer with a hard corner at the groove floor, which is the classic groove-crack initiator and is not what any moulded groove base looks like.
findings.fix: LUG_ROOT_FILLET = 0.055 and LUG_DRAFT = 0.030 (total root growth 0.085 m per side; 2.7 deg draft over the depth, and at reference scale a 0.008 m base radius on a 0.090 m non-skid, which is what a real one is). With the 0.356 m grooves from the tread-table fix that leaves a 0.186 m floor, floor/top = 0.52, correct for OTR. Then make the fillet an actual tangent quarter-round: insert a fifth ring between levels[0] and levels[1] at (fillet*0.29, -TREAD_DEPTH + fillet*0.71) so the two segments approximate a radius instead of a bevel.

findings.title: Port cut edge shows a crown laminate - belts in the sidewall of a radial
findings.problem: build_port cuts through the sidewall (PORT_INNER_RADIUS 9.382 to PORT_OUTER_RADIUS 13.153, thickness from sidewall_mid, so 0.30-0.40 m) and paints it with tire_laminate, whose band table is a CROWN section: 31.8% four-belt package, a 5.6% nylon cap ply, 8.6% undertread and a 14.2% tread cap. Belts stopping at the shoulder is the definition of a radial - that is what the R in 8400/80R580 means. Showing a belt package and a tread cap in a sidewall cut is the single most obvious construction error on the whole prop to anyone who has cut a tire open, and it is at the exact spot every player walks past. Secondary: spec.py's crown stack (CAVITY_RADIUS = GROOVE_RADIUS - UNDERTREAD - BELT_PACKAGE - LINER_THICKNESS) allocates zero gauge to casing plies, so even in the crown the texture's 23.6% casing band has nothing behind it.
findings.fix: Add a sidewall variant to tire_laminate (a crown=False branch, or a tire_laminate_sidewall family) with layers, cavity side to outside: liner 0.00-0.10, tie gum 0.10-0.16, casing ply 1 0.16-0.42, casing ply 2 0.42-0.62, sidewall rubber 0.62-1.00. One coarse cord row per casing ply at the existing 0.052 pitch; no belts, no cap ply, no tread cap. Point build_port's cut mesh at that material. Then the detail that would make it sing: the port perimeter's two roughly-circumferential edges cut ACROSS the radial cords (cord ends, dots - what the texture draws now), but the two roughly-radial edges cut ALONG them, so those should show continuous lengthwise strands. Split the cut mesh into two materials by |out_r| vs |out_t| in port_perimeter and rotate the UV 90 degrees on the radial edges. Finally add CASING_PLY = 0.010 * SCALE to spec.py's crown stack so the geometry and the texture agree.

findings.title: MAX LOAD scaled as a length instead of as an area - off by ~10x
findings.problem: 486000 kg is a reference load of ~69 t multiplied by SCALE (7.046). Load capacity is pressure times footprint area, so it scales as SCALE-squared, not SCALE. Cord force per unit width goes as p*r and cord strength per unit width goes as gauge, i.e. as SCALE, so the inflation pressure is scale-invariant at ~600 kPa and the load must go as area. It is also the one number on this sidewall that is not derived from anything, in a file whose entire stated method is that nothing is guessed. Alongside that, the print band is missing the two markings that identify an OTR tire on sight: the star rating (casing strength, * / ** / ***, on every earthmover sidewall) and the TKPH/TMPH heat rating, which is the marking most specific to this class and exists on no other kind of tire.
findings.fix: Derive it: REFERENCE_MAX_LOAD = 100_000.0 (a 59/80R63 at 600 kPa) and MAX_LOAD = REFERENCE_MAX_LOAD * SCALE**2 -> 4 965 000 kg. Print it the way a real sidewall does, with the pressure it is rated at: "MAX LOAD 4965000 kg AT 600 kPa COLD". Add "***" (three-star) to SERVICE_CODE so it reads "E-4 *** TL RADIAL", add a "TKPH 850" line, and add the approved rim, which the file already knows since MERIDIAN[0] fixes rim width at 0.746 x SW: "RIM 246.00/580" (or 306.00/457 after the size-code fix).

findings.title: Sidewall letters stand 15.6 mm proud at reference scale with zero draft
findings.problem: LETTER_RELIEF = 0.110 m divides back to 15.6 mm proud on a 4 m tire. Real moulded OTR sidewall type stands 3-6 mm. And curve.extrude with no bevel gives a straight prism: the letter walls are vertical, which no moulded letter can be - it would not release from the plate. In shoulder.jpg and sidewall_print.jpg the result is unmistakable, the type reads as separate plastic parts glued onto the sidewall, catching a hard specular on the vertical walls. This is the loudest wrong note in every sidewall close-up and it undoes the good decision to make the type real geometry rather than a normal map.
findings.fix: LETTER_RELIEF = 0.040 (5.7 mm at reference scale). Add curve.bevel_depth = spec.LETTER_RELIEF * 0.28 with curve.bevel_resolution = 1 before the convert, which gives the rounded, slightly-tapered crown a plate-moulded letter actually has. Keep LETTER_HEIGHT at 1.90 for legibility - the height is a defensible game-readability call, the relief is not. Optionally set the letters on a shallow recessed panel (drop sidewall_relief by 0.02 m over the BRAND_RADIUS +/- 1.1 band); that panel is a real feature and it reads at distance far better than extra relief does.

findings.title: Alternating zigzag sign makes lateral grooves alternate 0.36 m and 0.88 m
findings.problem: zig() bows the whole lug circumferentially by up to GROOVE_ZIGZAG at mid-row, leading and trailing edges together. Flipping the sign every pitch means adjacent lugs bow opposite ways, so lateral groove widths alternate 0.620 - 0.260 = 0.360 m and 0.620 + 0.260 = 0.880 m all the way round. That is a 42% swing, it is visible as an alternating wide/narrow rhythm in profile.jpg, and it adds materially to the voidy look flagged above. No mould produces it - a zigzag groove is a constant-width channel on a wandering path, which is the whole point of zigzagging it.
findings.fix: Drop the alternation: pass zigzag=spec.GROOVE_ZIGZAG unconditionally so every lug in a row bows the same way and the groove keeps constant width along a zigzag path. If you want circumferential variation instead, phase the zigzag with the pitch index continuously (math.sin(TAU * pitch_index / TREAD_PITCHES * 3)) rather than square-waving it.

findings.title: The bead is a semicircular bullnose - no seat taper, toe, heel or bundle
findings.problem: MERIDIAN has a single bead station and the generator closes it with a half-round cap swept across the 0.62 m shell thickness. With no rim in the build, both bead holes are wide open and prominent in hero.jpg, profile.jpg and scale.jpg - the bead area is one of the two things you actually look at from the front, and it is currently a smooth rubber lip. A real tubeless OTR bead has a 5-degree tapered bead SEAT, a defined heel radius where it sits in the flange, a toe that runs down toward the rim base with a slight undercut, and a visible circumferential bulge over the bead bundle. None of it is there, and the bead is the one area where a tire without a rim has to carry its own identity.
findings.fix: Add two meridian stations below the current lower-sidewall one: (0.000, 0.732) at the toe and (0.055, 0.760) at the heel, so the base runs on a 5-degree taper (heel radius larger than toe radius by 2 * seat_width * tan(5 deg), ~0.055 m here). Replace the half-round toe cap with: a flat tapered seat face across the base, a heel arc of ~0.30 m radius, a square-ish toe with a 0.08 m undercut on the inboard side, and a 0.10 m circumferential swell on the inboard face at 0.55-0.95 m above the base for the bead bundle. Keep the tire_bead chafer texture on all of it - the burnished polish band it already draws will then land where a rim flange actually bears.

findings.title: DOT TIN format is invalid in every regime
findings.problem: A TIN is DOT + plant code (2 characters historically, 3 alphanumeric under the 2025 NHTSA rule) + a 2-character size code + an optional manufacturer code of up to 4 + a 4-digit date. "XR9K" is a 4-character plant code, which is not valid under either the old or the new format, and "CLS8" then has to be both size and optional code. It is the kind of thing a tire person reads first because it is the only string on a sidewall with a defined grammar. Secondarily, an E-4 haul tire on a 63-inch rim is off-road equipment and is not a highway tire, so many real ones carry a manufacturer serial and a moulded week/year rather than a DOT TIN at all.
findings.fix: BUILD_CODE = "DOT XR9 K8 CLS8 3426" - 3-character plant XR9, 2-character size K8, optional manufacturer code CLS8, week 34 of 2026. Or, more authentic for the class, drop the DOT and use "SERIAL XR9K-CLS8-3426" plus a separate moulded "3426" date. The 3426 date itself is a nice touch and matches the repo date; keep it.

findings.title: Inner liner bladder lattice is 5-9x too coarse and isotropic on a radial
findings.problem: 26 cells over a 2.40 m tile is a 92 mm diamond pitch with 18 mm grooves at -0.42 height. A curing bladder's vent lattice is 6-20 mm across regardless of tire size - it is a bladder surface feature, not something that scales 7x with the casing. In cabin.jpg the cavity floor reads as industrial waffle plate rather than butyl, and it is the single largest surface in the whole interior. The construction is also isotropic in both diagonals, which telegraphs crossply; on a radial the strongest thing you see through the liner is the casing cords running bead-to-bead, i.e. a set of parallel lines across the cabin lane, plus a much finer near-circumferential set under the crown where the belts are.
findings.fix: lattice = 120.0 (20 mm pitch on the 2.40 m tile) and narrow the groove threshold from 0.20 to 0.10. Then add the cord telegraph, which is the feature that actually says 'radial': a low-amplitude sine along v only, ~0.045 m pitch (casing cord pitch x SCALE) at about 0.35 of the lattice's height amplitude, plus a second finer set along u at ~0.020 m pitch for the belts. Keep splices=2 and the talc - both are right.

findings.title: Stone ejectors are hemispherical domes; OTR stone protection is a wedge
findings.problem: add_ejector builds a hemisphere of radius 0.165 with a lifted apex. In tread_close.jpg it reads as a rivet or a mushroom sitting in the groove. Groove-base stone protection on earthmover tires is a tapered wedge or an intermittent ridge with a steep face on the entry side and a shallow ramp out, so a trapped stone is levered up rather than seated on a dome. A hemisphere is the light-truck idiom.
findings.fix: Replace the dome with a wedge: 0.42 m long circumferentially, spanning ~0.6 of the groove floor width, 0.20 m tall, with a ~70-degree face on the leading edge and a ~20-degree ramp trailing, and alternate the facing direction so the tire stays non-directional. Size it against the new groove floor from the root-flare fix so it fits (0.186 m floor -> keep the wedge base under 0.15 m wide). While in there: TWI bars exist in the groove floors (add_wear_indicator, 6 sets) but nothing on the shoulder locates them - add a small moulded TWI marker on the buttress at the six matching angles, since every tire with TWI bars carries an external locator.

findings.title: Two derived comments in spec.py are stale
findings.problem: REFERENCE_OD = 63*0.0254 + 2*(59*0.0254*0.80) evaluates to 3.99796 m, not the 4.0056 m in the trailing comment, and SCALE is therefore 7.0466, not the 7.033 in the comment. Everything downstream is computed from the expressions so no geometry is wrong - TREAD_DEPTH 0.6342, CAVITY_RADIUS 13.1523 and CAVITY_FLOOR_Z 0.9337 all check out against the stated measured facts. But this file's whole rhetorical position is that its numbers are consequences rather than taste, and two stale hand-written values in the derivation chain are the first thing a reviewer pulls on.
findings.fix: Change the comments to '= 3.998 m' and '~7.047'. Better, delete the hand-written values and emit them in the generator's log line so they cannot drift again - the pack already does this for the cage mass assert.

verdict_reason: The material *thinking* here is the best in the pack — the taxonomy (tread / sidewall / print / liner / laminate / bead as six distinct manufacturing surfaces) is exactly how a tire look-dev artist would break it down, and the vent spew, ozone-checking ridge network, bladder lattice and cut-edge cord package are all the right ideas, correctly constructed. But the maps as shipped do not deliver any of it, and the reason is measurable rather than a matter of taste. The tread colour PNG spans 15 of 256 code values (min 5, max 19); the sidewall spans 8. Every one of the seven roughness maps spans under a fifth of the 0–1 range (tread p5→p95 = 0.667→0.827; sidewall_print has a standard deviation of 5.3 bytes — it is a constant). The tread and sidewall normal maps have mean surface tilts of 1.3° and 3.5°, i.e. they are flat, because nothing authored into any tire map is finer than ~34 mm while the texel is 2.15 mm — three resolvable octaves are unused. On top of that, `_to_image` writes linear floats into a `.color` PNG that this repo has already *measured* the engine to decode as sRGB (AGENTS.md ~1752), so the tread the engine sees is 0.0035 linear where 0.043 was authored: 12.3x too dark, darker than any real material. The result is the shoulder and hero renders: a beautifully modelled, superbly lit charcoal *shape* whose surfaces read as unpainted clay. Add one 90-degree-wrong feature direction (the sidewall mould ripple runs radially), a bloom mask that is a flat 17% haze instead of a mask, seven black hairlines through the hero close-up detail (the port cut edge), and 320 mm diamond-plate teardrops on the walkway the player boards from. None of this is a redesign — it is one colour-space fix, about fifteen frequency/range constants, and one axis flag. Fixed, I think this would be genuinely staggering; shipped as-is it is not.
excellent: The family taxonomy is right and it is the whole reason this reads as a tire and not a black doughnut: separate tire_liner, tire_laminate, tire_bead and tire_sidewall_print, each keyed to a real manufacturing surface rather than one 'rubber' shader reused six ways. Do not collapse these.

texture_kit._spew — vent whiskers built as capsules with wrapped u/v offsets so they survive the tile seam. The observation in the docstring is correct (moulded vent spew is the cheapest 'this came out of a mould' tell and is nearly always missing) and the execution is clean. Only the whisker size is off; the mechanism should not be touched.

texture_kit._checking (crazing as the ridge set |n-0.5| of a value-noise field, giving closed branching polygonal cracks) and texture_kit._cord_row (each belt drawn at its own pitch, radius and phase so casing cord and belt cord differ). Both are the correct constructions — only their spatial frequencies are wrong, not their design.

The metric-UV discipline throughout: TILE_TREAD/TILE_SIDEWALL/TILE_LINER/TILE_STEEL, create_colossus_tire.ring_uv, blender_kit.add_metric_box_uvs, and the metric rewrite inside build_tongue. Texel density is genuinely uniform across a 28 m object; almost nothing at this scale gets that right.

Committing the sidewall type, rim line, protector ribs and buttress lug wrap to real extruded GEOMETRY instead of normal maps. shoulder.jpg is the strongest frame in the set and it is strongest exactly where the relief is real — the letters hold up under a raking light in a way no decal would.

texture_kit._rng (sha256 seeding) and _value_noise (true bilinear with Perlin fade, wrapped mod cells). Both sit upstream of every texture in the pack, both are correctly reasoned, and the second is why the tire has no lattice artefacts to complain about.

findings.title: Linear albedo written into an sRGB-decoded .color map: tire is 12x too dark
findings.problem: _to_image does `clip(array,0,1)*255` with no transfer function, so an authored linear 0.043 becomes byte 11. AGENTS.md ~L1752/~L1781 already establishes, measured on engine 0.39.4.0, that a `.color` map is decoded as sRGB. Measured on the shipped files: tread mean byte 11.5 (min 5, max 19), sidewall 13.9 (11-19), sidewall_print 12.5, liner 22.5. Decoded as sRGB those are linear 0.0035 / 0.0044 / 0.0039 / 0.0084 — the tread is 12.3x darker than the 0.043 that was authored and far below any real material (the darkest real surfaces sit around 0.02 linear). Worse, the entire tread albedo occupies 15 of 256 code values, so once harvested to a BC1 DDS the 5-bit endpoints collapse it into two or three flat colours and every bit of mould grain, polish and nick shading in the colour channel is destroyed. The Blender verify renders hide this because Filmic's log shadow roll-off compresses a 3.6-stop albedo error into a mild greyness.
findings.fix: sRGB-encode the colour map only (normal and _roughness.data stay linear). In build_set, before _save_stable of the colour: `c = np.where(c<=0.0031308, c*12.92, 1.055*np.power(c,1/2.4)-0.055)`. To keep the blast radius off the rest of the pack (and off harvested DDS hashes), gate it as `srgb: bool = False` on build_set and set `"srgb": True` on the seven tire palette entries first. Verify by re-measuring: tread colour mean should move 11.5 -> ~58, sidewall -> ~62, liner -> ~84, laminate cap -> ~58. Keep the authored linear bases as they are — 0.043 is the correct value for carbon-black tread compound, it is simply not being delivered. One hue note while you are in there: tread base (0.043, 0.042, 0.041) skews warm (R>G>B) while the code's own comment says carbon black 'skews very slightly blue'; make it (0.0400, 0.0415, 0.0445) and let the wax bloom carry the warm note, which is what actually happens on a real tire.

findings.title: Every roughness map is perceptually constant - the maps do no work
findings.problem: Measured p5->p95 spans on the shipped maps: tread 170->211 bytes (0.667->0.827), sidewall 139->163 (0.545->0.639), liner 117->147, laminate 120->162, bead 109->146, and sidewall_print 128->132 with a std of 5.3 bytes — a flat sheet. A tire's material identity in game is almost entirely roughness contrast (matte dusty groove rubber against a burnished contact crown against a waxy bloomed sidewall) and none of that contrast exists. The tread cause is that the mask and the amount are the same variable: `polish = clip((fbm-0.35)/0.5,0,1)*wear` caps at 0.42 with wear=0.42, so `rough + (1-polish)*0.20 - polish*0.16` can only reach 0.669 at its glossiest against 0.826 at its mattest.
findings.fix: Separate mask from amount everywhere. tire_tread: `pmask = np.clip((polish_fbm-0.35)/0.5,0,1)` kept at 0..1, then `roughness = 0.92 - pmask*wear*1.15 + cuts*0.06` (0.44 on a polished crown, 0.92 unworked, ~0.98 in a fresh cut — fresh torn rubber is the roughest thing on a tire); keep the colour lift on `pmask*wear` as it is. tire_sidewall: `roughness = 0.52 + wax*0.85 + crazing*0.35` (needs the wax fix below). tire_liner: `rough=0.30` and `dust*0.55` — butyl is the one glossy surface on a tire and the current map never gets below 0.41. tire_sidewall_print: the print is real geometry, so either drop the roughness map from that family entirely or give it the sidewall treatment.

findings.title: No feature finer than ~34 mm against a 2.15 mm texel; normal maps read flat
findings.where: texture_kit.py:tire_tread/tire_sidewall (base_cells args) and spec.py:PALETTE (L463-505, missing normal_strength)
findings.problem: At TILE_TREAD=2.20 m on 1024 px the texel is 2.15 mm (sidewall 2.54 mm), so features down to ~5 mm are resolvable. Authored: tread `fine` base_cells = size//48 = 21 cells = 105 mm; `micro` = size//16 = 64 = 34 mm; sidewall `radial` = size//64 = 16 = 162 mm, `fine` = size//24 = 42 = 62 mm; `_checking` cells = size//96 = 10 = 260 mm, i.e. ozone crazing at continent scale when real checking is 1-10 mm apart. Measured consequence on the shipped normal maps: tread mean surface tilt 1.3 deg / p95 2.3 deg, sidewall 3.5 / 6.1 — flat. Compare bead 9.8/28.9 and liner 9.6/29.3, which do read. This is why the tread crowns in tread_close.jpg look like smoothed clay: what you see is geometry shading plus nothing. Separately, prop_builder.py:321 already reads `texture.get("normal_strength", 2.0)` and not one of the seven tire palette entries sets it.
findings.fix: tire_tread: `fine = _fbm(size, rng, base_cells=max(64, size//10), octaves=3)` (102 cells = 21 mm, finest octave 408 cells = 5.4 mm) and raise the grain term from `(fine-0.5)*0.34*grain` to `*0.75*grain`. tire_sidewall: `radial` base_cells 16 -> 64 (40 mm), `fine` 42 -> 170 (15 mm), `_checking(size, rng, max(6, size//8), checking)` (128 cells = 20 mm) with octaves 2 so the top octave does not become white noise. Then add to spec.PALETTE: `"normal_strength": 4.0` on tread, 3.5 on sidewall, 3.0 on liner and bead, 2.5 on laminate, 3.0 on deck. Target on re-measure: mean tilt 8-14 deg, p95 ~30 deg on tread and sidewall.

findings.title: Sidewall mould ripple runs radially; it must be concentric
findings.where: texture_kit.py:tire_sidewall `ripple = np.abs(_stripes(size, ripples, axis=1) - 0.5)` (and the same line in tire_sidewall_print)
findings.problem: `_stripes(axis=1)` returns `np.tile(wave[None,:],(size,1))` — it varies along u and is constant along v, so its iso-lines are lines of constant u. The sidewall UV is create_colossus_tire.ring_uv -> u = radius*theta (arc length), v = radius. Constant u is therefore a RADIAL line on the tire. The shipped map puts 76 mm-pitch radial spokes on the sidewall, where a real one has concentric mould ripple. You can see them in shoulder.jpg and sidewall_print.jpg crossing the concentric protector ribs at an angle — the one cue that most reliably says 'tire sidewall' is 90 degrees wrong, and the docstring correctly states the opposite of what the code does ('ends up concentric with the tire - get that axis wrong and the sidewall reads as brushed metal').
findings.fix: Change `axis=1` to `axis=0` in tire_sidewall and in tire_sidewall_print's ripple line, and raise `ripples` 34.0 -> 104.0 (2.6/104 = 25 mm pitch, the real range; 104 need not divide 1024 since the stripe is periodic in count).

findings.title: Bladder lattice is 92 mm and reads as floor tile in the cabin
findings.problem: 2.40 m / 26 = 92 mm diamond cells. A real curing-bladder vent grid is 5-15 mm. Combined with the strongest normal in the set (measured p95 tilt 29.3 deg) it is by far the loudest thing in cabin.jpg, and because it is a regular grid at human-object scale it actively destroys the sense of size — the cavity of a 28 m tire reads as a tiled room. This is the largest single interior surface and the one the car spends the whole experience on.
findings.fix: `lattice=128.0` (2.40/128 = 18.7 mm, 8 px per cell, and 128 divides 1024 so the tile stays exact) and drop the groove depth `groove * -0.42` to `groove * -0.26` so at that pitch it is a whisper rather than a trench. Also raise the talc mottle frequency: `dust` currently uses base_cells = size//22 = 46 (52 mm blobs); make it size//4 = 256 (9 mm) so release dust reads as dust rather than as cloud.

findings.title: The wax bloom mask is not a mask - it is a flat 17% haze everywhere
findings.problem: The docstring calls this 'the whole trick' — antiozonant wax deposited in the recesses rather than sprayed uniformly. But the height field at that point has amplitude roughly +/-0.2, so `0.5 - height*1.4` spans about 0.22 to 0.78: it is a soft gradient covering every texel, not a mask selecting valleys. With bloom=0.34 the resulting wax term sits near 0.17 everywhere, which after the colour mix is a uniform ~+21% linear lift. The flagship idea in the family is not executing, and the roughness lift that is supposed to ride on it (`wax*0.26`) is likewise uniform, which is half of why the sidewall roughness map spans only 0.09.
findings.fix: Make it select: `recess = np.clip((0.02 - height) / 0.10, 0.0, 1.0) ** 1.5` so wax only lands in the ripple valleys and inside the checking cracks. Raise the `bloom` default 0.34 -> 0.60, the wax tint from [0.152,0.140,0.126] to [0.20,0.18,0.15], and mix at `wax*0.9` rather than `wax*0.55`. Bloom on a stored mining tire is a strong warm-grey film, several times the base albedo, not a 21% lift — and once it is a real mask you can also feed it into roughness at `+wax*0.85` without flattening the clean rubber.

findings.title: Laminate has a black hairline at all seven band interfaces
findings.problem: `_band(size, lo, hi, f)` returns `clip((v-lo)/f,0,1) * clip((hi-v)/f,0,1)`. At a boundary shared by two abutting bands, the upper band's second factor and the lower band's first factor are both exactly zero, so BOTH masks vanish and the accumulated colour there is 0. Measured row-means on the shipped laminate colour map: v=0.062 -> 3.21 (neighbours 27.2 / 17.7), v=0.104 -> 2.51 (20.7 / 26.3), v=0.340 -> 1.00 (30.8 / 17.1), v=0.398 -> 2.36, v=0.716 -> 1.71 (35.3 / 119.6), v=0.858 -> 2.25, plus 0.00 at the v wrap. That is seven 1-2 texel black lines drawn across the cut edge you framed a dedicated render (port_close.jpg) to show off.
findings.fix: Make the bands a partition of unity instead of a product of ramps: define `step(v, e) = np.clip((v - e)/f + 0.5, 0.0, 1.0)` and `mask = step(v, lo) - step(v, hi)`. Abutting masks then sum to exactly 1 at every boundary. Extend the topmost band's `hi` past 1.0 (or wrap the step) so the v=0/v=1 edge does not keep its black line either.

findings.title: The port cut shows a tread section, but the port is cut through the sidewall
findings.where: texture_kit.py:tire_laminate `layers` tuple, applied at spec.PORT_INNER_RADIUS 9.382 to PORT_OUTER_RADIUS 13.153
findings.problem: The access port lives entirely in the sidewall. The laminate stack nevertheless spends 0.398-0.716 (32% of the section) on a four-belt steel package, 0.716-0.772 on a nylon cap ply and 0.858-1.000 on tread cap. A radial tire has no belts, no cap ply and no undertread anywhere in the sidewall — those exist only under the crown. The section a sidewall cut actually exposes is inner liner, tie gum, one or two radial casing plies and sidewall compound, thickening toward the bead. Anyone who has stood next to a cut earthmover casing will read the current edge as wrong, and the cut edge is the single most 'expert' surface in the whole build, so it is the one place the error costs the most.
findings.fix: Add a `section="sidewall"` variant with layers: liner 0.00-0.10, tie gum 0.10-0.16, casing ply 1 0.16-0.38, casing ply 2 0.38-0.56, cushion gum 0.56-0.64, sidewall compound 0.64-1.00; two `_cord_row` calls only, centred at 0.27 and 0.47 at the coarse casing pitch, and delete the `fabric` cap-ply band and its weave. Keep the existing stack under `section="tread"` for a future crown cut. Bonus if you want it: radial casing cord runs radially, so on the circumferential runs of the port perimeter the cords cut end-on as dots (what `_cord_row` already draws) and on the radial runs they cut lengthwise as long parallel wires — worth a second variant on those faces.

findings.title: 320 mm diamond-plate teardrops on the walkway the player boards from
findings.problem: 1.60 m / 5 cells = 320 mm teardrops. Rolled tread plate is 25-60 mm. This is the surface directly under the camera in dock.jpg and port_close.jpg, next to correctly-scaled handrails and hazard chevrons, so it is one of the strongest scale-breaking cues in the set. build_tongue even carries a comment about having fixed 'a whole diamond plate tile on a 0.17 m step - 400 mm teardrops on a walkway' — the UV was made metric but `cells` was never revisited, so the oversize teardrops survived the fix. Measured deck normal p95 tilt is also only 9.9 deg, so the lugs barely emboss.
findings.fix: `cells=32.0` (1.60/32 = 50 mm, 32 px per cell, and 32 divides 1024 exactly so the tile stays clean). With the finer cell, raise `height = bump*0.42` to `bump*0.55` and add `"normal_strength": 3.0` to the deck palette entry. Also fix the hardcoded `((0,0),(0.3,0),(0.3,0.2),(0,0.2))` UVs on the tongue's side and end quads (create_colossus_tire.py ~L1053, ~L1063) so those faces match the metric scale of the deck they abut.

findings.title: Two spurious concentric parting lines per sidewall from a tiled map
findings.where: texture_kit.py:tire_sidewall `seam = np.exp(-(((v - seam_v)/0.006)**2)) * parting`, with parting=0.5 by default
findings.problem: v is `radius / TILE_SIDEWALL` and it tiles. The sidewall spans radius 7.366 to 13.153, i.e. v = 2.83 to 5.06, so `v mod 1 = 0.5` occurs at radius 9.10 m and 11.70 m: two raised 16 mm-wide concentric ridges per sidewall. A tire has exactly one parting line, at one chosen radius. This is the same class of mistake the generator already avoids correctly for the rim line and protector ribs, which are real geometry at RIM_LINE_RADIUS 8.25 and PROTECTOR_RADII (12.10, 12.72, 13.30).
findings.fix: Pass `"parting": 0.0` in the tire_sidewall palette params, and add the parting line to the geometry rib list at ~12.40 m with the same treatment as PROTECTOR_RADII (a ~0.05 m proud, ~0.04 m half-width rib). Anchored features belong in geometry here; only stationary-statistics detail belongs in a tiled map.

findings.title: Two families do not tile: measured 8.6x and 5.4x seam steps
findings.problem: Measured seam step against the median interior gradient: bead colour u-seam 8.6x and v-seam 8.4x, bead normal 3.2x both axes; laminate colour u-seam 5.4x, laminate normal u-seam 3.8x. Cause on the bead: `np.linspace(0, 44, 1024)` gives 23.27 texels per thread, so `np.floor(ramp)` boundaries do not land on texel boundaries and the last cell is a partial. Cause on the laminate: `(u/pitch + phase) % 1.0` only wraps cleanly when 1/pitch is an integer, and 1/0.052 = 19.23, 1/0.026 = 38.46, 1/0.034 = 29.41. The laminate wraps around the whole port perimeter, so its seam repeats at every 2.6 m of arc. Everything else in the set tiles well (tread 0.2x, sidewall 0.3x, liner 0.6x, deck 0.9x) — this is two constants, not a design problem.
findings.fix: tire_bead: `warp=weft=128` (which also lands the weave at a realistic ~20 mm thread pitch instead of the current 59 mm sacking). tire_laminate: snap the cord pitches to exact reciprocals — 0.052 -> 0.052632 (1/19), 0.026 -> 0.026316 (1/38), 0.034 -> 0.034483 (1/29).

findings.title: Palette roughness is dead; metallic silently makes rubber 25% metal
findings.problem: prop_builder writes `roughnessFactor` only in the `else` branch, i.e. only for materials with NO texture manifest. So `roughness: 0.62 / 0.54 / 0.5 / 0.46 / 0.55 / 0.48` on the six tire entries is inert — those numbers document nothing and cannot be used to tune anything, which is misleading for the next person. `metallicFactor` by contrast is always written, so `tire_laminate`'s `metallic: 0.25` makes the rubber gum in the cut edge 25% metal across its whole area (there is no metallic map), and `tire_bead`'s 0.1 does the same to the woven chafer. Rubber is a dielectric; anything between 0 and 1 in a metallic-roughness workflow is not a real material, and 0.25 metal darkens the diffuse and adds a tinted specular that is exactly wrong for gum. Separately the cord tint is neutral grey (0.62, 0.63, 0.66) while the layer comment correctly says 'brass-plated steel cord' — brass plating is the whole reason tire cord looks the way it does at a cut edge.
findings.fix: Set laminate and bead metallic to 0.0 (and hazard to 0.0 while you are there — painted steel is a dielectric). Recover the cord read from the map instead: `cord=(0.62, 0.50, 0.26)` for brass, and push the cord roughness term from `-steel*0.28` to `-steel*0.45` so the wires read as bright low-roughness specular against matte gum. Then either delete the dead `roughness` keys from the textured palette entries, or teach prop_builder to emit `roughnessFactor` alongside a roughnessMap so the number means something.

verdict_reason: The idea is the best thing in this pack: a 960-node free body that rolls only because a car pushes on its liner, measured (not scripted) by an exact three-point circumcentre fit that keeps working 300 m from a ref node bolted to the dock. The collision winding on the tire itself is verifiably right — I checked all 2838 triangles: 480 crown tris outward, 384 liner tris inward, zero duplicate triples, zero holes in the cavity floor at any probe. But I cannot be wowed by a machine whose front door does not exist. All six loading-dock deck triangles have normal z = -1.0000, so a car driving up the ramp falls straight through it; and the boarding gangway that bridges dock to port sill is visual-only geometry with no cage nodes and no collision at all — a probe down the entry corridor at y=0 finds NOTHING between x=-4.45 and x=-4.019, then a double-sided band that dives 0.672 m in 0.382 m, then a 0.46 m vertical wall up onto the liner. The rest compounds it: a linear static solve of the shipped jbeam puts 33 kN of COMPRESSION into two tie-downs whose beamDeform is 28 kN, which yields them on frame one and jacks the port side 37.7 mm off the ground so the Colossus spawns tilted, standing on two nodes; and the liner nodes — the exact surface the car drives on — sit at omega*dt = 2.037, past the symplectic-Euler limit, the highest in the whole pack. Every one of these is a few lines from being right, and the file already contains the helper (add_oriented_quad) that would have caught the worst of them.
excellent: add_oriented_quad (create_colossus_tire.py:1512) checking winding against MEASURED node positions instead of assuming it. I verified every triangle: 0 of 480 crown tris face inward, 0 of 384 liner tris face outward, 0 duplicate triples in 2838. The crown collides from outside and the liner from inside, exactly as required. Do not touch this function - extend its use.

nodeWorldPosition = vehicle:getPosition() + vehicle:getNodePosition(cid) (runtime.lua:203). This is the only formulation that survives the tire rolling 300 m away from a refNode bolted to a fixed dock and therefore never moving. getPosition stays at the dock, getNodePosition carries the delta, and the sum is the live node. Deliberate and correct.

fitAxle (spec.py:606) is the standard three-point circumcentre, algebraically exact - I checked a and b against the closed form alpha=|v2|^2*v1.(v1-v2)/(2D), beta=|v1|^2*v2.(v2-v1)/(2D) with D=|v1 x v2|^2, and they match term for term. Markers at stations 0/16/32 are exactly 120 deg apart, and markerAngle building its in-plane basis from the axis alone makes the reported angle immune to yaw.

portClock's angleZero trick: because marker 0 (crn_c_j00) and the port both start at the bottom, (tire.angle - angleZero) IS the port's clock angle with no extra bookkeeping. Free, exact, and it keeps working after the tire has rolled and yawed away.

The cavity floor. Probed on a 7x9 grid across the full 7.2 m lane including the port arc: a continuous upward-facing surface at every point, correct z, no holes, no down-facing ghost ceilings. The car cannot fall through the floor it drives on.

Refusing to drive the tire. 960 genuinely free nodes, LUA_BEHAVIOR applies zero forces/velocities/poses, and the whole runtime is read-only. That is the entire reason this prop is interesting and it must stay that way.

findings.title: All six dock deck collision triangles face DOWN; a car falls through the ramp
findings.problem: cage.add_quad([deck_l(i), deck_r(i), deck_r(i+1), deck_l(i+1)]) walks -y then +x, whose cross product is -Z. I computed the normals from the shipped jbeam: all 6 groundModel:"metal" triangles have normal z between -0.9975 and -1.0000. jbeam coltris are one-sided, so the entire 13 m ramp and landing is an invisible one-way floor that only collides from underneath. A probe at y=0 from x=-17.4 to x=-4.45 finds that down-facing deck and nothing else. This is the exact failure AGENTS.md:740-751 documents ("a car driving on thin air"), and the file's own add_oriented_quad exists to prevent it - but the dock quads bypass it.
findings.fix: Route the deck through the same guard the tire uses: add_oriented_quad(cage, [dock[('deck_l',i)], dock[('deck_r',i)], dock[('deck_r',i+1)], dock[('deck_l',i+1)]], Vector((0.0, 0.0, 1.0)), ground_model="metal"). Then add a static gate to tests/test_giant_props_pack.py asserting every triangle whose three nodes are all fixed:true has normal_z > 0 (or belongs to a both-sided pair) - the pack has 26 tests and none of them look at winding.

findings.title: Boarding gangway has no physics; port threshold is a 0.67 m ditch then a 0.46 m wall
findings.where: examples/giant_props/colossus_tire/blender/create_colossus_tire.py:1029 build_tongue (mesh only, never added to the cage) and :1727/:1744 (port collision skips)
findings.problem: build_tongue returns Blender meshes that go into tire_objects and get flexbody-bound; build_cage never creates a single tongue node or quad. Probing the entry corridor at y=0 walking inboard: x=-4.45 to -4.019 has NO collision surface whatsoever (0.43 m of nothing); x=-4.019 to -3.637 is the upp_r->shl_r sidewall band, double-sided, descending from z=1.142 to z=0.470 (a 60% downgrade into a pit); then a 0.464 m vertical step up to the liner floor at z=0.934 starting at x=-3.60. The cause of the last part is port_open_at (:248) testing the panel's MIDPOINT radius (13.28 for upp_r->shl_r) against [9.382, 13.153] instead of testing OVERLAP, so the panel straddling the sill is never cut; and the shoulder-band skip at :1727 is a blanket "station in port quads" rather than the same radius test, leaving a 40 mm slot at x=-3.637. Net: the car cannot board, which is the whole prop.
findings.fix: Three changes. (1) Give the tongue a real cage: 2 root node columns on the port sill ring and 2 tip columns at TONGUE_TIP_RADIUS/TONGUE_REACH_X, tied into the port_frame family, with add_oriented_quad(..., Vector((0,0,1)), ground_model="metal") decking so it is drivable and lifts away with the tire as designed. (2) Add a node ring at PORT_OUTER_RADIUS (= CAVITY_RADIUS) on the +X sidewall of cross_section() so the port's outer edge lands on a cage edge and the sill is genuinely flush. (3) Replace port_open_at's midpoint test with an overlap test (radius_hi >= PORT_INNER_RADIUS and radius_lo <= PORT_OUTER_RADIUS) and use that same predicate for the shoulder-band skip at :1727.

findings.title: Tie-downs sit in 33 kN compression at spawn (beamDeform 28 kN) and tilt the tire
findings.problem: I solved the shipped cage statically under gravity (linear axial stiffness, unilateral ground contact iterated to convergence). The tire settles 67.8 mm; the strap from fixed dock_l_0 to free max_r_j46 SHORTENS by 13.8 mm, so at beamSpring 2.4e6 it carries 33.0 kN of COMPRESSION. beamDeform is 28000, so both tie-downs plastically yield on frame one, before the player does anything - and a NORMAL beam is the wrong element for webbing, which cannot push at all. The knock-on is worse than the yield: those two compressed straps jack the port side up, so crn_cr_j00 (port side) floats 37.7 mm off the ground while crn_cl_j00 (far side) contacts. Delete the straps from the same solve and the settle is symmetric - both x=+-1.68 rows land at exactly the 58.8 mm crown drop. So the shipped Colossus spawns tilted 0.64 deg standing on 2 nodes over a one-sided 1.68 m strip instead of a symmetric 3.36 m base.
findings.fix: In STRAP_SPEC set beamSpring=3.0e5, beamDeform=60_000.0, beamStrength=95_000.0. That drops spawn compression to ~4 kN, closes the port-side gap from 37.7 mm to 10.6 mm (re-solved), and still gives ~250 kNm of restraint torque at the 2.66 m moment arm - three times the ~87 kNm a boarding car can apply. If BeamNG's tension-only beam type is available in 0.39.4, use it instead and keep the stiff spring; verify the exact beamType token against the game's own jbeams rather than guessing.

findings.title: Liner nodes run at omega*dt = 2.04 at 2000 Hz, past the integrator limit
findings.problem: A lin_c node masses 31000*0.11/240 = 14.21 kg and carries 6 belt beams at 18 MN/m (2 meridian, 2 hoop, 2 diagonal) plus 3 tread at 3 MN/m plus the inflation chord: sum(k) = 1.179e8 N/m. The tight Gershgorin bound for a mass-spring lattice, omega_max = sqrt(2*sum_k/m), gives 4073 rad/s, so omega*dt = 2.037 at dt=1/2000 - past the symplectic-Euler stability limit of 2. Damping is no help: c*dt/m = 1.126, also past the non-oscillatory bound. 147 of the 960 free nodes are at or over 2.0 and 240 are over 1.5, and they are precisely the surface a 1600 kg car parks its wheels on, so contact impulses excite the worst mode directly. Pack calibration from the same script: bouncy_castle 0.154, glass_atrium 0.344, pendulum_gauntlet 0.392, catapult_seesaw 1.773. This is the stiffest thing in the pack by a wide margin.
findings.fix: Divide the steel families by 4 in BEAM_SPECS: belt 18e6->4.5e6, bead 20e6->5e6, port_frame 24e6->6e6, tread 3e6->0.75e6. That takes the worst node to omega*dt ~1.02 and c*dt/m ~0.56. It costs nothing structurally: the ring's ovalisation under its own 3556 N/m self-weight goes from ~1.4 mm to ~5.6 mm on a 28 m body. Raising MASS_FRACTIONS["liner"] to ~0.25 at the crown's expense is the alternative, but softening is the better trade because it also fixes the contact patch.

findings.title: 31 tonnes rests on 2 contact nodes: the cage never deflects to reach the crown arc
findings.problem: The crown arc drops 58.8 mm at x=+-1.68 and 235 mm at x=+-3.36, so the outer tread rows only touch once the tire deflects that far. It does not: my static solve gives 67.8 mm of body settle and a converged contact set of exactly TWO nodes (crn_c_j00 and crn_cl_j00), spanning 1.68 m of axial width, one-sided. A 31 t body with its CoM at z=14.086 is balanced on a 1.68 m one-sided strip - max lean before the CoM leaves the base is 6.8 deg on the good side and ~0 on the other. It cannot fall back on gyroscopic self-righting either: for a hoop that needs v^2 > 1.5*g*R = 207, i.e. 14.4 m/s = 52 km/h, which is ABOVE the top band in BEHAVIOR.speed_bands (13 m/s = 47 km/h). At every speed the design anticipates, the Colossus stays up only on contact width it does not have. The spec says the tread family "flattens into a contact patch"; it flattens 68 mm.
findings.fix: Apply the steel/4 softening from the previous finding - I re-solved with it and the contact set grows from 2 nodes/1.68 m to 10 nodes spanning x=-1.68..+3.36 across three circumferential stations, which is a real footprint. If you also want the full 6.72 m tread carrying, raise TREAD_ARC_RADIUS from 24.0 to ~110 m so CROWN_DROP falls to 0.051 m, within the achievable settle. Do both and the tipping threshold goes from 6.8 deg to 13.4 deg.

findings.title: TIRE_MASS derivation counts one friction force twice; 30 km/h takes ~30 s, not 15 s
findings.problem: The two torque terms are the same force. A car resting on the liner transmits only its tangential friction f to the tire; the normal force N is radial and contributes zero moment. In equilibrium f = m*g*sin(phi) AND f <= mu_eff*N = mu_eff*m*g*cos(phi), so the traction line and the weight-moment line are the SAME constraint - they intersect at tan(phi) = 0.5*0.9 = 0.45, phi = 24.2 deg. Max torque is m*g*R_cav*sin(24.2) = 84.6 kNm, essentially the spec's first term. Adding the 92.9 kNm traction term on top double-counts by 2.07x. Using the true inertia measured from the shipped node cloud (I = 4.946e6 kg m^2, k_gyr = 12.63 m, not the quoted 12.15) the achieved alpha is 0.0176 rad/s^2 and 8.33 m/s takes 33.6 s. Even crediting the centripetal grip bonus once it moves (at 7.8 m/s liner speed N rises 52% and torque reaches ~120 kNm) the honest figure is ~29 s - roughly double the design target TIRE_MASS was solved from.
findings.fix: Either re-derive TIRE_MASS from the single correct torque: I_adm = 84.6e3/0.0394 = 2.15e6, mass = 2.15e6/12.63^2 = 13.4 t, rounded to ~15-16 t after crediting the speed-dependent grip; or keep 31 t and restate the design target honestly as "~30 s to 30 km/h". Do not keep both the 15 s claim and the 31 t number. Also correct k_gyr from 12.15 to the measured 12.63 m.

findings.title: insideTire is dead code, so occupancy freezes the instant the straps are cut
findings.problem: insideTire is defined - correctly, against the live fitted axle, precisely to solve the fact that a trigger box cannot follow a body that rolls 300 m - and is then never called. Both triggers are anchored to the fixed dock, and behavior.onExit returns early once b.released, so b.aboard and b.aboardCount are frozen from the release beat onward. After release the runtime cannot tell whether anyone is still inside: the "PORT IS DOWN - go now if you want out" callout fires at an empty carcass, colossus_tipped reports stale occupancy, and a player who bails out keeps getting revolution announcements.
findings.fix: In behavior.update, after `local tire = readTire(state)` succeeds and when b.released, sweep the known subject vehicles with insideTire(tire, vehicle) and rebuild b.aboard/b.aboardCount from that instead of from the trigger. Gate updateExitWindow on b.aboardCount > 0.

findings.title: refNodes are degenerate: left is parallel to back, up is 3.4 deg from horizontal
findings.problem: ref=(x2,0,0) and back=(x2,-3,0) differ only in authored Y, and left=dock_l_3 is at (x2,-4.2,0) - the same axis. In vehicle space left-ref = (0,4.2,0) and back-ref = (0,3,0): |fwd . left| = 1.000. up=dock_l_0 gives up-ref = (12.95,4.2,0.78), i.e. 3.4 deg off horizontal. I ran this across all 21 props: every other one is exactly 0.000 with up = [0,0,1]; colossus is the only degenerate table (pendulum_gauntlet is 0.984 and already known-marginal). The pack's own runtime survives because propFrame picks the best-conditioned PAIR (I ran test_giant_props_frame_math.py -k colossus: 4 passed), but BeamNG's engine-side transform - getRotation, getDirectionVectorUp, the orbit camera, spawn alignment - is built from these four nodes and orthogonalises to an "up" pointing along world +X, i.e. the prop reports itself rolled ~90 deg.
findings.fix: Author two dedicated datum nodes on the dock centreline and pass them: a left datum at authored (DOCK_RUN_X - 3.0, 0.0, 0.0) (maps to vehicle +X from ref) and an up datum at authored (DOCK_RUN_X, 0.0, 3.0). Add a pack-wide gate asserting |normalize(back-ref) . normalize(left-ref)| < 0.2 and normalize(up-ref).z > 0.9 - it would have caught pendulum_gauntlet too.

findings.title: FACET_SAGITTA prose says 18.9 mm; the code's own formula gives 30.2 mm
findings.problem: The comment justifies STATIONS=48 with "a 1.844 m facet chord whose sagitta is 0.0189 m", but OUTER_RADIUS*(1-cos(pi/48)) = 14.086*0.0021413 = 0.03016 m, and the chord check c^2/(8R) = 1.844^2/(8*14.086) agrees at 0.03017. The number in the prose is 1.6x low, and it is the number the resolution decision was made on. It matters physically because the cage barely deflects (68 mm), so the polygon is not smoothed out by the contact patch: at 8 m/s the tire turns at 0.568 rad/s and hands the player a 30 mm drop-and-catch at 4.34 Hz with 304 kN behind it.
findings.fix: Fix the comment to 0.0302 m. If 19 mm was genuinely the target, STATIONS must go to 60 (sagitta 0.0193 m, +240 free nodes) - but softening the steel families first is the cheaper cure, because a contact patch spanning three stations bridges the facets instead of dropping into them.

findings.title: cutStraps sets released=true even if the vehicle-VM break never runs, with no retry
findings.problem: pcall wraps prop:queueLuaCommand, which only fails if the QUEUE call errors - it returns success whether or not beamstate.breakBreakGroup('colossus_tiedown') actually executes in the vehicle VM. b.released is then set unconditionally, and both cutStraps (`if b.released then return end`) and onEnter (`if zone ~= "cabin" or b.released then return end`) close off every retry path. A single failed release leaves the player permanently strapped to the dock with the runtime insisting the tire is loose, and the only escape is a prop reset.
findings.fix: Do not set b.released in cutStraps. Set b.releaseRequested and b.releaseAt = b.clock, and in behavior.update confirm from the live cage: once (tire.centre - b.spawnCentre):length() > 0.5, or the two max_r strap-anchor nodes have moved relative to the dock, set b.released. If 2 s pass with no motion, re-issue the queueLuaCommand once and emitError(state, "strap_release_failed") on the second miss.

findings.title: The port_frame ring makes section stiffness asymmetric about the centre plane
findings.where: examples/giant_props/colossus_tire/spec.py:295 (port_frame 24e6) and create_colossus_tire.py:1552-1560 (frame_edges over 5 stations of the +X sidewall)
findings.problem: 40 beams at 24 MN/m replace casing/sidewall beams at 4e6/1.2e6 over five stations of the +X sidewall only. There is no counterpart on -X, so the carcass is measurably stiffer on the port side. In the static solve this shows up as part of the 0.64 deg spawn lean (the tie-down compression is the larger part). A permanent lean on a rolling hoop is a permanent steering input - the Colossus will trace a long arc rather than run straight, which is fine as flavour but is not authored, not documented, and not reproducible once the straps are fixed.
findings.fix: Either mirror the ring - emit the same port_frame family over the matching five stations of the -X sidewall as a balance ring (a real tire's opposite sidewall does carry the same bead/apex package) - or drop port_frame from 24e6 to 6e6 so the delta against casing is small. Then re-run the static solve and assert crn_cl_j00 and crn_cr_j00 land within 5 mm of each other; that assertion belongs next to the existing mass check in main().

verdict_reason: The craft here is real and I verified most of it rather than taking it on trust: all 12 texture sets regenerate pixel-identical under three PYTHONHASHSEEDs and match the checked-in PNGs exactly (maxdelta 0); the texture_kit change is one purely-additive hunk after potato_skin plus 8 FAMILIES lines, so none of the other 20 mods can drift a byte; a full ensure_textures + build_prop into a scratch copy reproduces the jbeam, materials, runtime.lua and bootstrap byte-for-byte; and the strap tether is a genuine authored connection whose removal leaves exactly two components (960 free tire, 16 fixed dock) - the tire is self-connected, which is the property that actually matters and which the pack's connectivity gate does NOT check. But I cannot be wowed by a change that lands the pack red and unshippable on day one. test_pack_has_all_mods fails right now (21 mods vs a literal 20) - the deliberate tripwire this pack maintains was not bumped. Worse, mod/vehicles/.../default.jpg and standard.jpg (sha ea922ef0...) are NOT copies of the checked-in authoring/ericrolph_colossus_tire_thumbnail.jpg (sha 0394a752...): the zip was cut at 22:27:19 and the last Blender run rewrote the thumbnail at 22:32:13, so build.py colossus_tire prop && dist from a clean checkout moves two members and produces a different sha256 than the checked-in lock. That is the Cannon Car Wash release-lock trap and the "dist is a RE-ZIP" hazard, both already written down in AGENTS.md, reproduced live. And the mass number the whole playability argument rests on is derived by adding two torques that are the same force counted twice. Fix those four and this is the best-documented mod in the pack.
excellent: Texture determinism is airtight and I measured it: all 12 colossus texture sets regenerate with maxdelta 0 against the checked-in PNGs, and the tire families produce identical hashes under PYTHONHASHSEED 0/1/42. Do not touch texture_kit.py's new families or _rng.

The texture_kit.py change is strictly additive - a single hunk inserted after potato_skin plus 8 lines in FAMILIES. No existing family's bytes can move, so the other 20 mods' harvests and zip locks are untouched. This is exactly how shared code should be extended.

Everything in mod/ except the two selector thumbnails regenerates byte-identical from spec.py + the handoff (verified by a full ensure_textures+build_prop into a scratch copy). The generated-never-hand-edited rule holds, and LUA_BEHAVIOR is embedded verbatim in runtime.lua.

The strap tether is a legitimate authored connection, not a fabricated graph edge: two real beams with beamDeform 28 kN / beamStrength 46 kN in their own breakGroup, modelled and textured, and cutting them leaves the 960 free tire nodes as ONE connected component and the 16 dock nodes as another. The v1 one-cage rule is satisfied honestly.

add_oriented_quad (create_colossus_tire.py:1512) checks collision-triangle winding against the measured node positions instead of assuming it - a one-sided jbeam triangle wound backwards is an invisible one-way floor, and this is the right defence.
SHIP_ASSETS = () with no assets/ directory at all, and the zip is 46 ZIP_STORED members on a single clamped timestamp with no .py/.glb/README. SHIP_ASSETS discipline is clean by construction.

findings.title: Mod-count tripwire not bumped: the static gate suite is red
findings.problem: MOD_KEYS discovers 21 directories with a spec.py now that colossus_tire exists, but the deliberate literal still asserts 20. `.venv/Scripts/python.exe -m pytest -q tests/test_giant_props_pack.py` fails: `assert 21 == 20`.
