This is the pack's own tripwire for a mod silently entering or leaving discovery, and adding a mod without bumping it is precisely the event it exists to force.
findings.fix: Change the assertion to `assert len(MOD_KEYS) == 21, MOD_KEYS` and extend the ledger comment above it in the established style: `20 -> 21 (2026-08-24): colossus_tire.` Also fix examples/giant_props/README.md line 3, which still says "Twenty oversized cartoon contraptions" - it is 21.

findings.title: Selector thumbnails are not derived from source; zip lock is unreproducible
findings.problem: prop_builder.build_prop (prop_builder.py:924-927) copies authoring/<mod_id>_thumbnail.jpg verbatim to default.jpg and standard.jpg. The shipped pair hashes to ea922ef02c6e7983 (13,698 bytes); the checked-in authoring thumbnail hashes to 0394a7523e1fe658 (13,687 bytes, pixel maxdelta 28). Then add the missing gate to tests/test_giant_props_pack.py: for every mod, assert sha256(mod/vehicles/<id>/default.jpg) == sha256(mod/vehicles/<id>/standard.jpg) == sha256(authoring/<id>_thumbnail.jpg). Nothing in the suite currently checks the derived thumbnail against its source.

findings.title: The mass derivation adds two torques that are the same force counted twice
findings.problem: The solve sums 'torque from the occupant's weight moment at a 25 deg climb angle' (87.2 kNm) and 'torque from its driven-axle traction' (92.9 kNm) to get 180.1 kNm. These are not independent. Free-body the car: the only torque it applies to the tire is the moment about the axle of the total contact reaction, which in quasi-static climb equals m*g*R_cav*sin(theta) = 87.2 kNm. Traction is not an additional source - it is the CONSTRAINT that decides whether theta is holdable (tan(theta) <= mu * driven-weight-fraction = 0.45, i.e. theta <= 24.2 deg, giving 84.8 kNm at the limit). Separately the quoted radius of gyration is wrong: computed from the shipped jbeam, I_axle = 4.946e6 kg m^2 at 31,000 kg, so k = 12.63 m, not the 12.15 m the comment states. Taking the spec's own (over-counted) 180.1 kNm with the real k already gives 28.6 t, not 31 t; with the correct single torque it gives ~13.9 t. The stated design target (1600 kg car, rest to 30 km/h in ~15 s) is not met by the shipped mass.
findings.fix: Rewrite the solve with one torque term. Either (a) keep 15 s / 30 km/h and land TIRE_MASS near 14,000 kg; or (b) keep 31 t and restate the target honestly - 31 t needs ~33 s to 30 km/h from a single midsize, or an AWD subject (mu * 1.0 -> theta <= 42 deg -> 138 kNm -> ~24 t), or two cars aboard; or (c) state the target as a torque-limited terminal behaviour rather than a time-to-speed. Quote the measured k = 12.63 m, not 12.15. Then add the assertion the target actually needs: main() already checks free_mass against MASS_TOTAL_TOLERANCE, but mass alone does not pin I - add an assert on sum(w*((y-cy)^2+(z-cz)^2))/M against an authored RADIUS_OF_GYRATION with a tolerance, so a meridian or CROWN_XS tweak cannot silently move the playability number.

findings.title: Tie-down webbing is skinned to the dock flexbody and stays welded to the quay
findings.problem: strap_ribbon() appends into build_dock's object list, so both straps land in the {MOD_ID}_visual mesh, which jbeam flexbodies row 1 binds to the {MOD_ID}_physics group - the 16 FIXED dock nodes. The physics beams, by contrast, run dock_l_0 -> max_r_j46 and dock_r_0 -> max_r_j02 on the free carcass. When the runtime breaks 'colossus_tiedown', the beams vanish and the tire rolls away, but the visible orange webbing - a rigid box spanning ~3 m out to authored x 4.77 on the sidewall - does not move at all. The player sees two straight orange planks cantilevered off the dock into empty air. This is the flexbody NODE SKINNING stage that AGENTS.md's pipeline-stage doctrine calls out, and no Blender render can show it because the renders never break anything. The docstring at :845-846 ('the webbing you see and the beam that holds the tire are one strap and not two') is true of the positions and false of the binding.
findings.fix: Split each ribbon at the point where the beam crosses: emit the dock-side half (anchor -> midpoint, plus the ratchet body) into dock_objects and the tire-side half (midpoint -> lug) into tire_objects, so the strap visibly parts and the tire-side tail rides away with the carcass. Simplest correct alternative: move the whole strap_ribbon output into tire_objects so the cut strap trails from the sidewall. Either way, update the strap_lug_points docstring to say the binding, not just the position. While there, tighten the lug: strap_lug_points returns theta = +-16.56 deg / r = 11.37 m while the cage anchors at station +-2 = +-15 deg / r = 11.398 m, ~0.31 m of arc apart - derive the lug from the same (key, station) the beam uses.

findings.title: No headless gate for a runtime whose whole job is nontrivial live geometry
findings.where: tests/ - zero files mention colossus (verified by grep -rln colossus tests/)
findings.problem: The pack's stated convention (README 'Validation', and the precedent of tests/test_hot_potato_logic.py and tests/test_spin_launch_sequence.py) is that a mod with real runtime mechanics gets a lupa gate against the REAL generated runtime.lua. colossus's runtime carries a three-point circumcentre solve (fitAxle), an axis-only orthonormal in-plane basis (markerAngle), an angle unwrapper, a revolution counter and a port clock. Every one of those is exactly identity-looking on a fresh unyawed spawn and wrong somewhere else - the same shape as the 2026-08-24 frame-convention bugs that tests/test_giant_props_frame_math.py was written for. Nothing exercises any of it. The static gates only see boilerplate and JSON shape.
findings.fix: Add tests/test_colossus_tire_sequence.py in the shape of test_spin_launch_sequence.py: load the generated runtime.lua under lupa against stubbed engine globals, then (1) feed three synthetic crown-node positions on a known circle and assert fitAxle recovers centre/axis/radius to 1e-6, including with the tire yawed 90 deg and tipped 30 deg; (2) drive markerAngle through a full synthetic revolution and assert unwrap/revolutions counts exactly 1 with no jump at the +-pi seam; (3) assert insideTire accepts a point on the liner and rejects one just outside cavity_radius + 1.2; (4) assert the boarding -> countdown -> cutStraps path emits colossus_released exactly once and is idempotent across a repeated onEnter.

findings.title: A strap that parts on its own leaves the runtime permanently silent
findings.problem: b.released only ever becomes true inside cutStraps, and cutStraps only runs off the boarding countdown. Two straps at beamStrength 46,000 N hold a body whose weight is 304 kN; a hard nudge, a settle onto the dock, or a subject entering fast can part them before anyone boards. There is no check that the group is still intact. Worse, cutStraps sets b.released = true purely on a successful pcall of queueLuaCommand, which is fire-and-forget and succeeds whether or not the vehicle Lua actually breaks anything. Either way the flag can disagree with the physics, and because announceSpeed, updateExitWindow and updateTipped are ALL gated on b.released, the entire reporting layer goes silent for the rest of the session with no error and no message - the exact failure mode that makes the prop look broken while every gate stays green.
findings.fix: In behavior.update, once tire state is available and b.released is false, compare tire.centre against the centre captured on the first frame (store it alongside b.angleZero). If it has moved more than ~0.6 m, set b.released = true, b.releasedAt = b.clock, showMessage a 'the tie-downs have parted' line, and emitEvent(state, 'W', 'colossus_released', {reason = 'strap_parted'}). Make cutStraps set b.released through the same path so there is one place that decides the tire is loose.

findings.title: Nothing gates that BEHAVIOR node and breakGroup names resolve in the jbeam
findings.problem: The runtime's whole measurement layer depends on three string literals - ericrolph_colossus_tire_crn_c_j00/_j16/_j32 - and on the breakGroup name 'colossus_tiedown'. If the generator renames a cage node column (say crn_c -> crown_c), readTire returns nil on every frame forever, behavior.update returns early, and NOTHING fails: the jbeam still matches the handoff, connectivity still passes, the zip still matches the lock, and the prop is silently inert. Same for the break group: if the beam extra is dropped, cutStraps is a no-op that still reports success. catapult_seesaw carries 100 such node-name references, so this gate is pack-wide useful, not colossus-only.
findings.fix: Add a parametrized gate: walk every string leaf of handoff['behavior'] that starts with f'{MOD_ID}_' and assert it is a node id in the shipped jbeam; and assert every breakGroup name appearing in the runtime.lua text (or in spec's *_BREAK_GROUP constants) appears on at least one beam's options in the jbeam. Both are pure JSON reads and cost nothing.

findings.title: Dead seeded RNG, with a comment asserting determinism never exercised
findings.problem: `import random` and `RNG = random.Random(20260824)` are never used - grep for `RNG.` returns nothing. The comment above it reads 'One seeded generator for every cosmetic jitter in the file. Seeded once and consumed in a fixed order, so the mesh is byte-identical run to run.' There is no cosmetic jitter in the file; the geometry is fully analytic. A future maintainer reading that comment will believe there is randomness to preserve and will reason about consumption order that does not exist. Of the 21 generators in the pack only hot_potato actually uses RNG, so this is leftover scaffolding. Two more dead names sit alongside it: sidewall_surface (:139, a one-line passthrough to sidewall_mid) and R_O in authoring/verify_render.py:35.
findings.fix: Delete line 25 and lines 53-55, delete sidewall_surface at :139 (its would-be callers already call sidewall_mid directly), and delete R_O from verify_render.py:35.

findings.title: The comment justifying STATIONS = 48 quotes a sagitta 60% below the formula
findings.problem: The comment says '48 stations is 7.5 deg apart: a 1.844 m facet chord whose sagitta is 0.0189 m, i.e. the collision cylinder is round to within 19 mm over a 28 m tire.' The chord is right (1.8425 m) but FACET_SAGITTA = OUTER_RADIUS * (1 - cos(pi/48)) = 0.03016 m - 30 mm, not 19 mm. 0.0189 m corresponds to about 61 stations. The number in prose is the entire justification for the chosen resolution and it disagrees with the formula printed immediately below it. FACET_SAGITTA itself is then never referenced anywhere in the pack.
findings.fix: Change the comment to quote 0.030 m (still a perfectly good 0.21% of radius - the conclusion survives, only the figure is wrong), and either use FACET_SAGITTA (e.g. assert it stays under a stated ceiling in the generator's main()) or delete the constant.

findings.title: PORT_INNER_RADIUS is a literal whose comment claims it is a derived value
findings.problem: `PORT_INNER_RADIUS = 9.382  # = MERIDIAN[1] radius`. It happens to equal BEAD_RADIUS + 0.300*SECTION_HEIGHT = 9.382 today, but it is typed, not computed. The spec's own opening thesis is 'Every radius below is derived from those three numbers, so the moulded lettering and the mesh can never disagree.' Change MERIDIAN[1][0] from 0.300 and the port sill silently detaches from the meridian station it is supposed to land on, with no assertion anywhere.
findings.fix: `PORT_INNER_RADIUS = meridian_point(*MERIDIAN[1])[1]` (move it below the meridian_point definition, or inline `BEAD_RADIUS + MERIDIAN[1][0] * SECTION_HEIGHT`). While auditing, PROTECTOR_RADII, RIM_LINE_RADIUS, BRAND_RADIUS and SIZE_RADIUS are also bare metres on a tire whose size is parametric - at minimum add an assert that each lies inside (BEAD_RADIUS, GROOVE_RADIUS).

findings.title: Hard-coded fractional UVs break metric texel density on tread faces
findings.problem: The lug crowns and buttress fronts are UV'd metrically (`radius * theta / TILE_TREAD`, e.g. :673-677, :726-728), but the buttress side caps and bottom lip, the tie-bar sides, the whole wear indicator and the stone ejector use literal spans like ((0,0),(0.3,0),(0.3,0.3),(0,0.3)) and ((0,0),(0.1,0),(0.1,0.1),(0,0.1)). At TILE_TREAD = 2.20 m a 0.3 span is 0.66 m, so a buttress cap that actually spans BUTTRESS_DROP = 1.55 m of radius gets its mould grain stretched ~2.3x, and the grain size visibly jumps across the edge onto the adjacent metrically-mapped face. This is the Cannon Car Wash 'tiny blocks' lesson the pack README explicitly codifies, applied inconsistently inside one generator.
findings.fix: Replace each literal UV tuple with the same metric expression used for the neighbouring faces - u = radius*theta/TILE_TREAD, v = x/TILE_TREAD for the axial direction, and for the vertical side faces v = (radius - radius_base)/TILE_TREAD. The dead `ring_uv(theta, radius, axial, tile)` helper at :232 is already exactly this function; use it rather than deleting it.

findings.title: Dead runtime state and inert tunables ship in the generated runtime.lua
findings.problem: Six BEHAVIOR keys are declared and never read by the Lua: marker_stations, outer_radius, port_span_deg, port_station, section_half, tire_mass. Of the keys that ARE read, exit_warn_deg drives a branch whose only effect is setting b.exitWarned, which nothing reads and which behavior.init never clears; and record_min_m maintains b.best, which is never shown, never emitted and never compared to anything - a 'record' with no output path. b.releasedAt is written and never read. Separately, portClock's 'zero = straight down' is not derived from the declared port_station at all: it uses b.angleZero, the angle of marker j00 on the first measured frame, which only equals the port's clock position because PORT_STATIONS = 4 happens to be centred on station 0. Change PORT_STATIONS to an odd number or move the port and the exit-window callouts are silently wrong with nothing failing.
findings.fix: Delete the six unread keys and b.releasedAt, and either finish or remove the record (emit colossus_record with b.best on tipped/reset, or drop b.best and record_min_m). Either implement a real early warning off exit_warn_deg (a 'port coming round' showMessage, with b.exitWarned cleared in behavior.init) or delete both the key and the branch. Make portClock derive its zero from B.port_station so the declared tunable is the thing that controls the behaviour.

verdict_reason: At 60 m this is genuinely striking — scale.jpg and profile.jpg have real presence, the variable-pitch tread reads as a designed tread rather than a repeat, and the port/dock/gangway staging is a great idea executed with care. But I audited the exported DAE directly and the model is inside-out: 100% of the 32,640 outer-sidewall triangles, 100% of the 4,032 cavity-floor triangles and the 11,232 inner-sidewall triangles are wound backwards. In Blender that only makes the sidewalls read flat and lifeless (it is exactly why cabin.jpg looks like an exterior shot); in BeamNG, which backface-culls flexbodies, the player will see straight through both sidewalls and drive on an invisible floor. AGENTS.md lines 735-751 warn about this failure mode in explicit terms — "Blender does not backface-cull; BeamNG does. Headless renders CANNOT catch an inside-out surface... Deriving a quad's winding by hand is error-prone" — and this generator derives every quad by hand, runs recalc_face_normals only on the lettering, and renders without use_backface_culling. Separately, the marquee close-up feature is broken: the size code and the pattern name are moulded into overlapping radial bands, so on both sidewalls and all three copies two strings are extruded through each other into illegible glyph soup (visible in shoulder.jpg, buttress.jpg, sidewall_print.jpg). And 28.2% of the whole polygon budget — 39,936 triangles, half of them with collapsed UVs — went to that lettering, while the carcass cut edge that spec.py spends forty lines justifying gets 112 triangles and the entire access port plus gangway gets ~2,350. You cannot stop and stare at a model whose hero close-up is unreadable and whose interior is invisible in the engine it ships to. The bones are excellent; the surface QA never happened.
excellent: Tread base + lug construction (build_tread / add_lug): every lug, tie bar, ejector and wear indicator sits its open bottom ring exactly on base_r(x) with no bottom cap, so a lathe carrying 180 lugs, 180 tie bars and 72 ejectors has ZERO coplanar overlap and zero z-fighting anywhere. Do not 'fix' the open bottom rings — they are the reason this works.

Tread UV uses a CONSTANT spec.GROOVE_RADIUS * theta / TILE_TREAD. Measured: 1.16:1 anisotropy, 2.25 m/tile dead uniform across the whole tread. This is the correct pattern and it is the model the sidewall must be changed to copy — do not touch it.

meridian_fractions() clustering 9 extra samples across each relief feature (rim line + 3 protector ribs) on top of the uniform 1/22 ladder. A 0.24 m rib on a 6.72 m meridian is 3.5% of it; this is the only reason the ribs survive at all. Keep it.

pitch_angles() normalising the PITCH_RATIOS onto 2*pi so the 36-pitch variable sequence closes exactly. Verified: no wrap seam in the pitch itself, and it is why the tread reads as a designed pattern rather than a repeat in profile.jpg and scale.jpg.

The port cut edge orientation and its v 1->0 mapping (build_port): measured 0 of 112 triangles face away from the doorway, and the v direction matches the laminate texture's liner-first row order. The logic is right; only its resolution is wrong.

The lettering's per-side mirror, theta = centre - side * local.x / band_radius plus bmesh recalc_face_normals (build_lettering). Verified correct on BOTH sidewalls: dot(exported normal, winding normal) = +0.990 with frac<0 = 0.000, and COLOSSUS reads correctly at the top of the +X wall in hero.jpg. The mirror question is settled — do not re-derive it.

findings.title: Both sidewalls, both inner faces and the cavity floor are wound inside-out
findings.where: blender/create_colossus_tire.py:348-349 (band calls), :405 (liner crown quad), :445-449 (fillet side test)
findings.problem: Measured on the exported DAE: outer sidewall lathe n_x*sign(x) = -0.890 with frac<0 = 1.000 across all 32,640 triangles (sample at x=+4.322 has winding normal (-0.995,-0.002,-0.104)); cavity floor n.radial = +1.000 with frac>0 = 1.000 across all 4,032 triangles (sample at z=0.938, the floor the car drives on, has normal (0.000,-0.022,-1.000) — pointing at the ground); inner sidewall n_x*sign(x) = +0.860 across 11,232 triangles; the shoulder fillet n_x*sign(x) = +0.939. Exported normals track the winding exactly (dot = +0.997, frac<0 = 0.000), so shading is inverted too. The bead toe is the one lathe that is right (n.radial -0.855, n_x*sgn(x) +0.314) purely because toe_rows traverses outer-face-to-inner-face and reverses the handedness by accident. In Blender this only makes the sidewalls read flat and dark (cabin.jpg renders the interior as an exterior because the floor's normal faces the world background); in BeamNG, which backface-culls flexbodies, you see through both sidewalls and drive on an invisible floor. AGENTS.md:735-751 documents this exact trap and mandates a build-time winding assert plus use_backface_culling in headless renders — neither is present.
findings.fix: Flip four things and nothing else: line 348 band(outer, rows_out, TILE_SIDEWALL, side < 0) -> side > 0; line 349 band(inner, rows_in, TILE_LINER, side > 0) -> side < 0; line 405 liner.quad(a, b, c, d, uv, smooth=True) -> liner.quad(d, c, b, a, uv, smooth=True); and swap the two branches of the fillet's `if side > 0`. Leave the bead toe alone — it measures correct. Then add the AGENTS.md gate so this can never recur: after each Mesh.build(), assert the area-weighted mean of (face normal . outward reference) > 0, where outward is +sign(x)*X for the outer sidewall, -sign(x)*X for the inner, -radial for the liner crown, +radial for the tread; and set `m.use_backface_culling = True` on every material in authoring/verify_render.py so the headless renders can see the hole.

findings.title: Size code and pattern name share a radial band and interpenetrate
findings.problem: SIZE_CODE sits at SIZE_RADIUS = 8.75 with height LETTER_HEIGHT*0.66 = 1.254 m, align_y=CENTER, so it spans radius 8.123-9.377. PATTERN_NAME sits at BRAND_RADIUS - 1.35 = 8.95 with height LETTER_HEIGHT*0.44 = 0.836 m, spanning 8.532-9.368 — entirely inside the size code's band, at the same angular centre, at the same standoff and the same 0.110 m relief. The two extruded meshes are driven straight through each other, on both sidewalls, on all three BRAND_COPIES: six collisions per tire. Crops of shoulder.jpg and sidewall_print.jpg show '8400/80R580' with the risers of 'TERRAVOLT RM-1' punching up through it — the middle line of type is unreadable glyph soup. This is the feature the whole sidewall_print render exists to show. BRAND also grazes it: BRAND spans 9.35-11.25, overlapping the size code by 27 mm.
findings.fix: Stop hand-picking band radii and derive them so bands cannot collide. Replace the three literal radii with a downward layout from BRAND_RADIUS: keep BRAND at 10.30 (span 9.35-11.25); place PATTERN_NAME centre at 8.85 (span 8.43-9.27); place SIZE_CODE centre at 7.85 with height*0.66 (span 7.22-8.48); place BUILD_CODE centre at 6.95. Then add an assert in build_lettering that, for each sidewall, the sorted (centre - height/2, centre + height/2) intervals are pairwise disjoint with >= 0.15 m of clear rubber, and raise if not. Note SIZE_CODE's current lower half also straddles the RIM_LINE_RADIUS 8.25 rib (8.12-8.38); the new radii clear that too.

findings.title: Sidewall UV shears without bound with theta and the seam does not close
findings.where: blender/create_colossus_tire.py:334-338 (band uv, `radius_lo * theta0 / tile`); ring_uv at :232 is now dead code
findings.problem: U is the per-ROW radius times theta, so adjacent meridian rows drift apart by (delta_r * theta)/tile. Measured UV stretch ratio (ratio of singular values of the surface->UV Jacobian) on the outer sidewall: median 9.37:1, p90 28.11:1, max 42.61:1, varying smoothly around the tire from ~2:1 in one quadrant to ~26:1 in the opposite one. The liner group hits max 42.53:1 on the inner sidewall (its crown and fillet, which use a constant R_CAV, are clean at 1.07:1). Compare the tread, which uses a constant GROOVE_RADIUS and measures 1.16:1. This is why the sidewall's mould texture renders as smeared diagonal streaks whose angle changes as you walk around the tire (sidewall_print.jpg, buttress.jpg) and why the liner's square bladder lattice reads as long streaks in port_close.jpg. Separately, at max section radius 11.398 the wrap is 2*pi*11.398/2.60 = 27.54 tiles, so the texture misses closure by 0.54 tile = 1.40 m — a ragged, radius-varying seam sitting at theta=0, i.e. the contact patch, which rotates into view the moment the tire rolls.
findings.fix: Make U a function of theta ONLY, with an integer tile count so the seam closes. In band(), replace the four U terms with `N * theta / TAU` where `N = round(TAU * R_REF / tile)` and R_REF = 0.5*(R_BEAD + OUTER_RADIUS) = 10.726 (N = 26 for TILE_SIDEWALL, 28 for TILE_LINER). Keep the new `arc_lo / tile` V — that part is already right. Result: zero shear, a seam that closes exactly, and a 2:1 density gradient bead-to-shoulder that is invisible on a noise-dominated rubber texture. Apply the same round-to-integer to the tread base while you are there (GROOVE_RADIUS*TAU/2.20 = 38.42 -> N = 38) so the tread texture closes too.

findings.title: 28% of the budget is lettering; the cut edge gets 112 triangles
findings.where: exported DAE material split; blender/create_colossus_tire.py:1149 build_lettering vs :835 build_port
findings.problem: Measured budget of the 141,676 exported triangles: tread 45,016 (31.8%), sidewall_print i.e. the moulded lettering 39,936 (28.2%), sidewall lathe 32,640 (23.0%), liner 14,112, bead toe 3,456, steel — the ENTIRE port bezel, 46 bolts, 10 gussets, 4 lift lugs and the tongue ribs — 1,804 (1.3%), tongue plate 304, tongue kerbs 128, and the port cut edge laminate 112 (0.08%). So the rolled bead toe, a feature 6.7 m up inside the bead hole that no player will ever be near, gets 31x the triangles of the cut edge, which spec.py justifies with forty lines of prose about the laminate being in true proportion and which is the surface the player's headlights hit at 2 m when they drive in. The cut edge is currently ONE flat quad band across its full 0.624 m section: a plank with a texture on it, which is exactly what the spec says it must not be. Meanwhile 39,936 triangles of Arial went onto a surface where half of them (see the UV finding) cannot even shade correctly.
findings.fix: Three reallocations, roughly budget-neutral. (1) Cut resolution_u on the letter curves from 3 to 2 — recovers ~15k triangles with no visible loss at 1.9 m cap height. (2) Cut the bead toe from steps=6 to steps=3 and use 72 stations on that ring alone: recovers ~2,300. (3) Spend it on the cut edge: step port_perimeter's cross-section into the five real laminate layers the spec already derives — LINER_THICKNESS 0.032, casing, BELT_PACKAGE 0.211, UNDERTREAD 0.056, tread cap — as 5 rings with 10-20 mm reveals instead of 1, i.e. ~560 triangles instead of 112, plus a bead-bundle bulge where the cut passes near PORT_INNER_RADIUS, and give the bezel box section 4 columns per face rather than 1. That single change does more for the close-up than the entire lettering budget does.

findings.title: 544 exactly-zero-area triangles shipped, all from the buttress bottom lip
findings.where: blender/create_colossus_tire.py:657 (`relief = spec.BUTTRESS_RELIEF * (1.0 - t * t)`) and :699-711 (bottom lip)
findings.problem: At t = 1 the relief taper evaluates to exactly 0, so outer_row and inner_row of rows[-1] are coincident vertex-for-vertex. The bottom-lip quads then span two pairs of identical points and the last band of side faces collapses to a line. Measured in the DAE: 544 triangles with area < 1e-9, every one of them at radius 12.298-12.404 and |x| 4.307-4.319, which is exactly BUTTRESS_DROP = 1.55 below the crown. Zero-area triangles produce a degenerate tangent basis, and BeamNG's normal-mapped shading on a degenerate tangent is the classic source of black speckle on an otherwise clean surface. Mesh.face's guard (`if len(set(indices)) != len(indices): return`) cannot catch these because it tests index duplication and every corner gets a fresh vertex() call — the guard is dead code.
findings.fix: End the taper at a real thickness instead of zero: `relief = spec.BUTTRESS_RELIEF * (1.0 - t * t) * 0.88 + 0.028` so the wrap terminates on a 28 mm moulded edge (which is also what a real buttress wrap does — it feathers, it does not vanish). That makes the bottom lip and the last side band non-degenerate and correct. Additionally change Mesh.face's guard to test POSITION duplication (drop the face if any two corners are within 1e-5 m) so the next collapse is caught at build time instead of shipping.

findings.title: tire_sidewall's mould ripple runs radially, not concentrically
findings.where: proplib/texture_kit.py:3489 `_stripes(size, ripples, axis=1)`; same bug at :3576 in tire_sidewall_print
findings.problem: _stripes(size, count, axis=1) tiles wave[None,:], so the value varies along the COLUMN index — lines of constant value are VERTICAL in texture space. On the sidewall U is circumferential, so constant-U lines are RADIAL SPOKES. The docstring says the opposite: 'ripples runs along u because the generator maps u circumferentially on the sidewall lathe, so the mould ripple ends up concentric with the tire - which is the direction it runs on a real one. Get that axis wrong and the sidewall reads as brushed metal.' The reasoning is inverted — a feature that VARIES along u produces lines PERPENDICULAR to u. Confirmed by opening the generated normal map: 34 clean vertical stripes. The parting-line seam in the same function is the one feature built on the v axis and therefore correctly concentric, so the two are fighting each other. Compounded with the UV shear above, this is what produces the sheared diagonal grain across every sidewall render.
findings.fix: Change both calls to axis=0 so the ripple varies with v and the resulting lines run concentric with the tire. Also fix the parting line while you are in there: with V now on metric meridian arc (arc/2.60), the sidewall's 7.0 m meridian spans 2.7 tiles, so the single mould parting line repeats 2-3 times per sidewall. Either move the seam out of the tiling texture and into geometry (one ridge in sidewall_relief() at a chosen radius), or drop `parting` to 0 in the palette entry for this mod.

findings.title: Stone ejectors pierce the lug skirts; the groove floor is 10 mm wide
findings.problem: Each lug's level-0 ring grows by LUG_ROOT_FILLET + LUG_DRAFT = 0.225 m per side. The shoulder groove spans |x| 2.200-2.660, i.e. 0.460 m, so the two flanking skirts consume 0.450 m of it and the actual groove FLOOR is 10 mm wide. The inner groove (0.660-1.160) leaves 50 mm. STONE_EJECTOR_R = 0.165, so every one of the 72 ejectors is a 0.33 m dome dropped into a 0.01-0.05 m floor: it interpenetrates both adjacent lugs by ~0.16 m with a raw, unbooleaned intersection line. A crop of tread_close.jpg shows this plainly — the ejector reads as a wad of gum stuck to the lug flank, half-buried, and it is smooth-shaded while everything around it is flat, so it also reads as a different material. Secondary defect: add_ejector puts its base ring at `base_r(x)` (the centre's floor radius) while the true floor at x +/- 0.165 is base_r(x +/- 0.165), so the ring floats or sinks by up to 17 mm around its circumference.
findings.fix: Two changes. (1) Replace the dome with the shape a real E-4 stone ejector actually is: a transverse wedge that spans the groove floor and wedges against both lug walls — a 4-point base loop from x=lo to x=hi at base_r(x) per corner, rising to a ridge at base_r + 0.20, ~24 triangles instead of ~80. That fixes the interpenetration by construction (it is MEANT to touch both walls), fixes the floating base ring, drops ~5k triangles, and looks right. (2) Widen the grooves so they are grooves: change TREAD_ROWS to ((0.000, 0.620), (1.320, 2.140), (2.760, 3.360)) giving 0.70 m and 0.62 m grooves, which leaves 0.25 m and 0.17 m of real floor after the skirts. Emit the ejectors flat-shaded (mesh.quad default) like every other moulded face.

findings.title: A 0.21 m open sidewall fin stands proud of the tread crown on both shoulders
findings.where: blender/create_colossus_tire.py:288-295 shell() driven by meridian_fractions() up to fraction 1.0; spec.py:222-229 MERIDIAN ends at 0.930
findings.problem: spec.MERIDIAN's last station is at fraction 0.930, and sidewall_mid() clamps to that value for everything above it, so the outer lathe runs from radius 13.616 to OUTER_RADIUS = 14.086 at a FIXED |x| = 3.867. The tread crown at that x is crown_r(3.867) = 13.774. Measured in the DAE: 576 outer-sidewall triangles sit above the crown, at |x| = 3.867 exactly, reaching r = 13.981 — a zero-thickness flange standing 0.207 m proud of the tread all the way around both shoulders, terminating in a free 144-edge circle per side (part of the 780 boundary edges the weld analysis finds at r 13.69-14.20). It is the bright rib visible outboard of the shoulder lugs in profile.jpg and hero.jpg. In BeamNG with backface culling it will be a ring that flickers in and out as the camera crosses its plane.
findings.fix: Terminate the lathe where it actually meets the tread envelope instead of at fraction 1.0. In meridian_fractions(), solve for the fraction f* at which shell(f, side, 'outer') satisfies radius >= crown_r(half) — with the current MERIDIAN that is f* = (13.774 - 7.366)/6.720 = 0.9536 — and clamp the fraction list to [0, f*]. Then stitch the lathe's top ring to the tread base surface's x = +/-TREAD_HALF edge with one band of quads (2 x 144 quads, ~576 triangles, i.e. exactly what the fin currently wastes) so the shoulder is closed rather than open. That also removes the 0.83 m unmodelled gap between the tread base edge at x = 3.360 and the sidewall shell.

findings.title: Both gangway kerbs hang 0.184 m off the tongue plate, with open ends
findings.problem: The kerb cross-section is built from `theta` to `theta + direction * 0.014` where theta is thetas[0] = -half_arc for direction -1 and thetas[columns] = +half_arc for direction +1. In both cases the offset moves AWAY from the plate, so the entire 0.014 rad * 13.15 m = 0.184 m kerb sits outboard of the plate edge with nothing beneath it — the daylight under the striped bar in port.jpg, dock.jpg and port_close.jpg. Separately the sweep is `for corner in range(4): nxt = (corner+1) % 4` with no cap at step 0 or step 8, so both ends are open tubes; the root end additionally starts at x_start = 3.411, i.e. 0.30 m inboard of the sill, so an open box end is left hanging over the cavity floor pointing into the cabin.
findings.fix: Change the offset sign so the kerb sits ON the plate: use `theta - direction * 0.014` for the second pair of corners. Then cap both ends — emit rows[0] as a quad wound outward and rows[steps] wound inward, 4 extra triangles total.

findings.title: Hardcoded non-metric UVs on buttress, kerbs, tie bars, TWIs, ejectors, bolts
findings.problem: add_buttress sets v = 0.0 -> 0.4 for EVERY one of its 5 bands instead of accumulating, so the tread texture restarts five times down each wrap: five hard horizontal texture seams on the single most recognisable silhouette feature of the tire, at 0.775 m/tile in V against the tread's 2.20 m/tile in U — a 2.8:1 anisotropy plus a visible band edge, both readable in buttress.jpg. The tongue kerb's hardcoded ((0,0),(0.5,0),(0.5,0.4),(0,0.4)) per step gives a measured 0.461 m/tile against the dock kerb's 0.963 m/tile — the same hazard stripe at two different scales, side by side in the same frame in dock.jpg. add_lug's side walls divide U by perimeter INDEX (index/count * lug_arc) even though the 18 perimeter segments have four different real lengths, so the block's ends and sides get different texel scales.
findings.fix: Do for these what the tongue plate already does correctly. Buttress: accumulate v as cumulative meridian arc, `v = arc_from_top / TILE_TREAD`, and carry it across bands. Kerb: `u = along-length distance / TILE_STEEL`, `v = cross-section arc / TILE_STEEL`, matching the dock kerb's metric_uv=(TILE_STEEL, TILE_STEEL). add_lug: accumulate U as the real perimeter arc length instead of index/count, and make the three V levels proportional to their true heights (fillet, TREAD_DEPTH-fillet-chamfer, chamfer*sqrt2) instead of TREAD_DEPTH/3 each. Tie bar / TWI / ejector / bolt: divide the real dimension by TILE_TREAD or TILE_STEEL.

findings.title: 19,784 lettering triangles have collapsed UVs; letter texel scale is 6.5x the sidewall
findings.where: blender/create_colossus_tire.py:1240-1266 build_lettering (no UV layer authored after convert/bend)
findings.problem: The font objects are converted to mesh and bent vertex-by-vertex, but no UV is ever authored, so the export carries Blender's auto-UV from the curve: measured 19,784 of the 39,936 sidewall_print triangles (49.5%) have exactly zero UV area — the letter cap fills. A zero-area UV triangle has a degenerate tangent basis, so the normal map on half the lettering is undefined in BeamNG. The half that does have UVs measures a median 2.508 tiles/m = 0.399 m/tile against the surrounding sidewall's 2.600 m/tile — a 6.5x texel-scale jump at every letter edge, so the rubber grain visibly changes scale where the type starts (readable in the sidewall_print.jpg crop).
findings.fix: After the bend loop, overwrite the UV layer with the same metric projection the sidewall uses, so the letter surface and the rubber it sits on are one continuous material: for each loop, u = N * theta / TAU with the same N chosen in the shear fix, v = (cumulative meridian arc at that radius) / TILE_SIDEWALL, and point the letters at the sidewall material rather than a separate sidewall_print family (keep sidewall_print for the small-print band where the text IS the texture). That kills the degenerate tangents and the scale jump in one change.

findings.title: Port bolts read as a serrated edge; opening corners square, frame corners rounded
findings.where: blender/create_colossus_tire.py:1121 add_bolt (called at :930 with height 0.095); :773-836 port_perimeter
findings.problem: 46 hex bolts at 0.135 m across flats and only 0.095 m tall, at 0.42 m pitch on a 0.62 m plate that is itself viewed nearly edge-on, do not read as fasteners — the crop of port.jpg shows them as a sawtooth chewing the bezel's silhouette, which is the single ugliest thing in the render set. They also stand along +X while the profile row they sit on is the tented ridge (width*0.5, proud + depth*0.35), so each hex leans out of its plate and half-overhangs. Separately, port_perimeter's corner smoothing only blends the OUTWARD DIRECTION over span=3 points; the perimeter points themselves stay on a hard rectangle. So the cut opening has 90-degree corners while the bezel's outer boundary is rounded — a mismatch that reads as an error, and a square corner is a stress raiser nobody would cut into a carcass.
findings.fix: Bolts: halve PORT_BOLTS to 24, raise the head to 0.19 m with a 0.22 m washer flange under it, and place them on the FLAT of the face plate by inserting a flat row into the profile tuple at (width*0.5, proud + depth*0.35) with two neighbours at the same stand, then orienting each bolt along that row's surface normal rather than +X. Same triangle count, an order of magnitude more read. Corners: in port_perimeter, replace the four straight edges with four edges plus four 0.60 m fillet arcs, moving the POINTS onto the arc, so the cut edge, the bezel inner lip and the bezel outer edge are concentric.
